parties:
Farookh Sobhan
Vs.
Abul Hossain being dead his heirs mosammat rokeya begum and others
full_judgment:
Mir Hashmat Ali, J: In the instant Rule the petitioner challenged the Judgment and decree dated 28.06.2009 and 07.07.2009 respectively passed by learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 542 of 2005 and the judgment and decree dated 27.07.2005 and 03.09.2005 respectively passed by learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 836 of 1981. 

 2. The predecessor of opposite party No.1 Abul Hossain instituted Title Suit No. 836 of 1981 for specific of performance of contract against the defendant-petitioner No. 1. 

 3. Short facts of the plaintiff's case is that defendant No.1 being owner of the schedule property entered into an agreement for sale of the schedule properties with the plaintiff at a consideration of Tk. 4,00,000/- (four lacs)on 21.08.1979 and the plaintiff paid Tk.45,000/- and the Defendant no.1 received the same as earnest / advance money and agreed to sale the schedule properties to the plaintiff within 90 days from the date of agreement. Subsequently on 20.09.1979 the plaintiff again paid an amount of Tk.50,000/- (fifty thousand) to the defendant No.1 on the request of the defendant No.1 before expiry of 90 days of the agreement and the defendant No. 1 acknowledged the same by making an endorsement in his own hand on the back side of the agreement. Subsequently after expiry of the period defendant No.1 received Tk.1,00,000/- on 02.07.1980 and Tk.20,000/- on 25.08.1980 and made endorsement of both the payment in the back side of the agreement. In this way, the defendant No.1 received Tk.215,000/- out of total consideration of Tk.4,00,000/- from the plaintiff. The plaintiff requested the defendant No.1 on several occasions to execute and register the sale deed but the defendant deferred on various plea. Lastly on 15.06.1991 the defendant No.1 refused to execute and register the sale deed and claimed higher amount. Consequently, the plaintiff filed the suit for specific performance of contract on 12.11.1981 and obtained solenama decree. Subsequently, the plaintiff filed Title Suit no, 239 of 1984 against the said solenama decree and obtained a decree on 27.06.1991. 

 5. Thereafter the plaintiff filed a civil petition for Leave to Appeal No. 343 of 1995 before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court and after hearing, the said Civil Appeal No. 54 of 1997 was allowed vide judgment and order dated 10.06.1999 and the compromise decree dated 15.09.1982 was set aside and Title Suit No. 836 of 1981 was restored to its original file and number. 

 6. After restoration, the defendant No.1 filed written statement denying materials assertion made in the plaint stating that the suit is not maintainable and that no cause of action was there for filing the suit. The suit is barred by limitation, the suit is bad for defect of parties and that alleged contract is not enforceable which is hardship for the defendant and that the suit property originally belonged to the father of the defendant No.1 Khondker Fazle Sobhan, Ex Ambassador and the suit property devolved upon all the heirs of original owner and they never executed any contract nor they are party to the proceeding. 

 12. Further case is that one Razia Zamal and Momenullah filed 2 suits against the defendant No.1 claiming title over some part of the suit land and obtained decree and as such the suit land does not remain the property of the defendant No.1, before starting the suit afresh. 

 13. Further case of the defendant is that the value of the suit property has been raised and that the defendant No. 1 has no right, title, interest over the suit property and that the defendant No.1 will suffer hardship. Further case of the defendant is that the plaintiff did not came before the Court with clean hands and as such the plaintiff is not entitle to get any relief and the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 14. The suit came up for trial before the Court of learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka and at the time of trial, one of the heir of the plaintiff Md. Sirajul Hoque was examined as P.W.1 and produced documents exhibit-'1, 2, 3 , 3(a) and 4' and the defendant No.1 examined 2 witnesses D.W.1 M.A. Salam D.W.2 Khalilur Rahman and also produced some documents which are marked exhibit —"A, B, C, D, D(1), E and E(1) and subsequently deed of sale in favour of Ambia Khatun and Babul Chowdhury has been marked as exhibit-`X and Y' respectively and also filed a Photostat of possession certificate, (original of which is in the record of Title Appeal No. 356 of 1994). 

 15. After hearing the learned Advocates of both the parties and considering the materials on record, the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 27.07.2005 and 03.09.2005 in Title Suit No. 836 of 1981. 

 16. Being aggrieved, the defendant No. 1 preferred Title Appeal No. 542 of 2005 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka which was eventually transferred to the Court of learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka. 

 17. After hearing the learned Advocates of both the parties and considering the materials on record, the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka dismissed the appeal by his judgment and decree dated 28.06.2009 and 07.07.2009 respectively in Title Appeal No. 542 of 2005. 

 20. He further submits that no where in the plaint nor in the deposition of P.W. 1 that the plaintiff alleged that he never offered the balance consideration amount and asked the defendant No.1 to execute and register deed of sale within the time fixed in the contract or thereafter and as such there is no cause of action and as such the plaintiff is not entitled to get a decree in a suit for specific performance of contract. He further submits that there is no evidence that the plaintiff ever ready or willing to perform his part of his contract nor any stamp paper was purchased by the plaintiff or deposited any amount by way of challan to get the stamp paper and as such the plaintiff was never willing to get the property registered within the stipulated period of 90 days and as such the plaintiff is not entitled to get any relief. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Silver Estate Limited —Vs- Abdul Hakim Mia and others reported in 43 DLR-360. 

 21. He further submits that after compromise of the matter between the parties, the defendant No.1 already transferred the suit property by executing and registering the sale deed and as such the defendant No. 1 has no right, title, interest, over the suit property and as such the defendant No.1 can not be directed to execute and register the suit property by way of specific performance of contract which means hardship and that the specific performance of contract is a discretionary relief of the Court and such discretion should be awarded judiciously in favour of the defendant and as such both the Courts below committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Moslimuddin Ahmed and others -Vs-Chandra Nath Ghosh and others reported in 6 BLC (AD)-139 and the case of Administrator of Waqfs and another -Vs- Musammat Sahera Begum Chowdhurani and others reported in 28 DLR-238, the case of Rakhal Dasi Rajakini -Vs- Ayesha Khatun Chowdhury and another reported in 1985 BLD. (AD)-49, the case of Jogesh Chandra Das & others -Vs- Farida Hasan reported in 1983 BLD (AD)- 225 and the case of Ram Chandra Das and others -Vs- Md. Khalilur Rahman and another reported in 1985 BLD (AD) 41. 

 31. He further submits that the trial Court as well as the lower appellate Court was influenced by the judgment and order of earlier Civil Appeal No. 54 of 1997 passed by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court and as such the judgment and decree passed by both the Courts below are liable to be set aside. He further submits that the schedule property after the transfer to the 3rd parties does not remain the property of the defendant No.1 and he has no right, title and possession in the suit property and that the right, title and possession of the property are of the 3rd party. One Razia Zamal and Momenullah filed suit regarding the same schedule property and obtained decree from the court but both the Courts below failed to consider the same thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 32. He further submits that the plaintiff did not came to execute the agreement as he found that the defendant No-1 is not in possession and he has no right, title and interest and as such the reported case Anwara Begum -Vs- Md. Karimul Haque and others reported in 5 BLC (AD)-119 is not applicable. 

 46. Furthermore, the plaintiff entered into the contract knowing fully well that the defendant No.1 is not in possession of the property. But after words he did not came forward to pay the rest amount within the period of time. Furthermore, the defendant No.1 after the compromise decree transferred the property to 3rd party but said compromise decree was set aside and restored the suit (after the transfer). According to Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act if any property transferred to 3rd party during the pendency of the suit it is hit by the doctrine of lispendence but in the instant case, initially the suit was decreed on compromise (previously) and after compromise the defendant No.1 petitioner entered into agreement with the 3rd parties and transferred the properties. Also gave some lands to the plaintiff according to the compromise decree as such the doctrine of lispendence is not applicable. Since by this time the value of the property increased for which the plaintiff filed a suit for setting aside the compromise decree. The matter went up to the Appellate Division and lastly the said compromise decree was set aside and the initial suit was restored to its position in the year 1995. But in the mean time before such restoration the defendant No.1 entered into the agreement with 3rd party on various occasions to sale the properties and executed and registered transfer deed in their favour and as such the right, title, interest and possession of the suit property was not with the defendant-petitioner (and as such transfer to 3rd parties are not hit by the doctrine of lispendence). 

 47. Furthermore one Razia Zamal and Momenullah filed 2 suits claiming over some part of the suit land and obtained decree even if a decree is obtained against the defendant No.1 that decree is not executable and court should not pass any decree which cannot be executed and court should not direct any person to execute the deed who has no existing transferable right, title and possession over the property. Furthermore, the plaintiff was aware that the defendant entered into a contract for sale of the property, which he is not in his possession and as such the contract is not a lawful contract and an unlawful contract is not enforceable in law. Since the decree is not executable decree, the doctrine of hardship came into operation. Since the defendant-petitioner has no right, title, interest and possession over the property, he has hardship to execute the document and that he cannot be directed to do an illegal act, thing or deed. 

 57. The Judgment and decree dated 28.06.2009 and 07.07.2009 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 542 of 2005 and the judgment and decree dated 27.07.2005 and 03.09.2005 respectively passed by the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 836 of 1981 are hereby set aside and the suit is dismissed.

parties:
Amena Khatun ----- Appellant
Vs.
Chairman Court of Settlement and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
SK Sinha J :Leave was granted to consider whether, the learned Judges of the High Court Division were justified in holding that the listing of the disputed property as abandoned property is not hit by proviso (a) to section 5 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance,1985 (Ordinance No.LIV of 1985) since the appellant has obtained decrees in Title Suit Nos. 1013 of  1980, 408 of 1982 and  213 of  1982from competent civil Courts prior to the date of inclusion of the disputed property in the abandoned property list on 23rd September, 1986 

 2. Facts relevant for the disposal of this appeal are that appellant entered into a contract for purchase of the disputed property on 22nd December, 1970 with the owner Jalal Uddin Khan and made part payment out of the consideration money, but the owner did not execute the sale deed despite repeated demands in that regard. Consequently, the appellant instituted Title Suit No.1013 of 1980 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for specific performance of contract and got a decree, and in pursuance of an execution proceeding she obtained a sale deed on 19th November, 1982 executed and registered through Court. Thereupon she approached the Ministry of Works for mutation of her name but the Ministry directed her to establish her title over the property. Pursuant thereto the appellant instituted Title Suit NoA08 of 1982 in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for declaration of title in respect of the suit property and ultimately the suit was decreed ex-parte on 28th June, 1983. The government subsequently filed Miscellaneous Case No.40of 1986 for setting aside the ex-parte decree but the said case was also dismissed on 22nd October, 1991 as being time barred. 

 3. Thereupon, the appellant renewed her prayer for mutation but she was informed that the property was already included in the list of abandoned property; she then instituted Title Suit No. 213 of 1985 in the 1st Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka for declaration that the disputed property is not an abandoned property and for direction upon the government for mutation of her name in respect of the said property. The said suit was also decreed ex-parte on 3rd March, 1986. As the appellant's prayers were repeatedly unheeded, she instituted Settlement Case Nos.21 and 22 of 1992 before the Court of Settlement, Dhaka. The Court of Settlement by judgment and order dated 28th April, 1992 rejected the application. The appellant thereupon unsuccessfully moved a writ petition in the High Court Division and then obtained leave from this Court to consider the above point. 

 4. Respondent No.2 contested the writ petition by filing an affidavit-in-opposition controverting the material averments made in the petition stating inter alia that the original lessee of the disputed property left this country during the War or Liberation keeping it uncared for. The property was found abandoned condition and the government treated it as abandoned property under PO No.16 or 1972 and has been managing the property through different tenants. Its further case is that since the property has already been declared as abandoned property any transfer of the same subsequent there- after is void and barred under Article 6 of PO No.16 of 1972, and the appellant collusively obtained those decrees and that those decrees do not cover under any of the clauses (a) or (b) of the proviso to section 5 of the Ordinance. 

 5. The Court of Settlement on consideration of the documents including the decrees filed by the appellant in support of her title held that they did not establish her title, that she did not file the original allotment letter and the contract tor sale with Jamaluddin which should have been in her possession if she has entered into such contract for purchase, that she did not explain the cause tor filing other two suits after obtaining the sale deed, that the appellant failed to satisfy that in those suits tile inclusion of the property in the abandoned property list was an Issue, and that she failed to prove her possession, and the original lessee Jamaluddin was in this country in 1972. 

 6. The learned Judges of the High Court Division visited the judgment of the Court or Settlement and other materials on record, and held that the materials on record proved that from 22nd December, 1970 to 19th November, 1979 the appellant had no title over the disputed property as she failed to produce any legal document conferring her title of the disputed property by the real owner, that the contract for sale does not confer any title of the property upon the petitioner, that she failed to prove that Jamaluddin was in Bangladesh on 28th February, 1972 and his whereabouts was not known to the Government when the property was declared abandoned property, that since the decrees in the suits were obtained after 28th February, 1972 they were hit by Articles 6 and 14(1) of PO 16 of 1972, that the decree in Title Suit No.213 of 1985 being based upon the ex-parte decree passed in a suit for specific performance, could not be pleaded for exclusion of the property from the list of abandoned property, that the subsequent decrees would not be a bar for inclusion of the property as abandoned property and that the appellant failed to produce the original contract for sale allegedly entered with Jamaluddin and the original lease deed before the Court of Settlement and thus the Court of Settlement was justified in rejecting the appellant's petition. 

 7. Learned Counsel appearing for the appellant argued that in view of the decrees passed in title Suit Nos.113 of 1980, 408 of 1982 and 2 13 of 1985, the learned Judges of the High Court Division erred in law in not holding that the listing of the disputed property is hit by section 5 of Ordinance No.LIV of 1985. Learned counsel further contended that since the appellant is still in possession of the disputed property, the learned Judges of the High Court Division erred in law in not holding that the listing of the disputed property is hit by proviso (a) of section 5 of Ordinance No.LIV of 1985. 

 It is now settled that a decree passed in a suit for specific performance of contract does not cover under any clauses of the proviso to section 5 of Ordinance No.LIV of 1985. It is not a decree declaring the title of the claimant since in such a decree the Court does not declare that the building is not an abandoned property or that the property has not been vested in the government under PO 16 of 1972. In a decree for specific performance of contract the main issue is whether the owner of the property entered into a contract for sale of the property. There is no scope for deciding the title of the plaintiff in such a suit. Reference in this connection is the cases of CQMH Md Ayub All vs Bangladesh, 47 DLR (AD) 71, Hosne Ara Begum vs Chairman, Court of Settlement, 46 DLR (AD) 9 and Go/am Rabbani vs Chairman, Court of Settlement, 13 MLR (AD) 345. If a property is vested in the Government as abandoned property under PO 16 of 1972, it shall be exempt from all legal processes in view of Article 14 of PO 16 of 1972 and thus, the transfer of the ownership of the property through Court would be null and void in view of Article 6 of PO 16 of 1972. 

 9. Now, the question is whether in view of the exparte decree passed in title Suit No.213 of 1985 declaring the disputed property as not abandoned property, the publication of the list including the disputed property is hit by proviso (b) to section 5 of the Ordinance. In order to bring the case within the purview of proviso (b) to section 5 of the Ordinance, the suit, appeal, or other legal proceeding must be one in which the vesting in, or possession of, the Government of the property as abandoned property under PO 16 of 1972 must be called in question whatsoever or any prayer has been made for return, restoration or transfer of the property by the Government or by any officer or authority subordinate to it to any person. The appellant's suit being one for declaration that 'the property is not abandoned property' proviso (b) of Section 5 is also not attracted in this case. 

 10. Section 5(2) of the Ordinance provides that the list published under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence on the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and has vested as such in the government. Section 7 provides that a person claiming any right, title or interest in any such building may make an application to the Court of Settlement for exclusion of the building from the list on the ground that the building is not abandoned one and not vested in the government under PO No.16 of 1972 or that his right or interest in the building has not been affected by the provisions of that order. As soon as a gazette notification is published enlisting the property as abandoned property there is presumption that the property has been legally included in list as abandoned property and any person claiming any right or interest in the said property must prove that the property is not an abandoned property in accordance with law and the vesting of it under PO 16 of 1972 has affected his/her right. The onus is absolutely on the person claiming the property and not on the Government. In other words, it is on the person who challenges that the property is not abandoned property or vested in the Government in accordance with PO No. 16 of 1972 is not the person who challenges the presumption. These provisions clearly show that the onus lies upon the person claiming the building or property as not abandoned property and that the government has no obligation to prove anything in support of its claim. 

 11. There is no statement either in the writ petition as to when the property was enlisted as abandoned property under section 5(1) of the Ordinance. The fact that the property is included in the list is proof of its being abandoned property and the Government has nothing to prove in support of such enlistment. The appellant failed to produce legal evidence in support her claim that after obtaining the decree in Title Suit No.213 of 1985 the property was enlisted under Section 5(1). However, from the decree passed on 1st February, 1986 it is apparent that the property was enlisted before the decree was passed.

parties:
Gopinath Das and others  ------ Plaintiff-Petitioners
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
M. Moazzam Husain, J: This rule was issued at the instance of the plaintiffs calling in question the judgment and order dated 11.3.2008 passed by the joint district judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Misc. Case No. 30 of 2007 under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure ("the Code" for short) setting aside a decree passed ex parte in Title Suit No. 724 of 1985. 

 3. The suit is for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession of 5.18 acre land described in schedule "B" of the plaint which forms part of 7.25 acre land in Mouza Sahar Dhaka (latterly Mouza Ramna). The land appertaining to the suit khatian originally belonged to one Gobinda Chanra Basak, shortly, "GC Basak". His name was initially shown in the CS record as মধ্যসত্বাধিকারী out of mistake. .Later by a correction case No. 24 of 1918 under section 198A of Bengal Tenancy Act his right was recorded as 'owner-in-possession'. G C Basak settled 5.18 acre agricultural land out of the land of said khatian with Gowranga Chandra Das, the original plaintiff and one Md. Noor Hossain, his benamdar by an amalnama executed on 24'rh Falgun, 1339 BS which is covered by CS plot Nos. 36,40,47,48, 52 and 82 as described in schedule B at an annual rent of Tk. 57/-. 

 8. Since settlement plaintiff No. 1 has been in possession of the B schedule land as a tenant by paying rent to the sherista of GC Basak upto 1362 BS. He did the act of possession by rearing and catching fish in low-lying area while in the remaining land he used to grow crops sometimes by himself and sometimes through bargadars. He also developed a portion of land by spending huge amount of money. GC Basak left for Calcutta around 1359 BS where he died shortly thereafter. His only son Rashik Lal Basak also permanently settled in India. The property belonging to GC Basak used to be looked after by Sudhangshu Shekhor Chatterjee who also left the country after acquisition of rent receiving interest. In the aforesaid premises the plaintiffs acquired an indefeasible title in B schedule property by virtue of settlement and by adverse possession in assertion of hostile title for a period much more that 12 years. 

 10. fit course of the proceedings plaintiff came to know that defendant Nos. 10-17 obtained a decree .dated 7-2-1975 in Title Suit No. 31 of 1966 from 6th Court of Munsif, Dhaka, for permanent injunction in respect of 0.98 acre land of CS plot No. 40 against the government and another on the plea of settlement taken from. Rashik Lal which was affirmed in appeal although the plaintiff was the rightful owner and have all along been in possession of the same The said decree is fraudulent and collusive. 

 11. The defendant No.1 served notice in 1980 upon defendant Nos. 3-9 under Act X of 1953 for surrendering possession of 0.20 acre of CS plot Nos. 82; 0.17 acre of CS plot No.1 and 0.15 acre of CS plot No. 48 treating the same as government khas land and the said defendant Nos.3-9 instituted Title Suit No. 37 of 1981 in the 5th Court of Sub Judge, Dhaka, for permanent injunction on the plea that they got the land by korfa settlement from Rashik Lal and Mohadev Chandra Goala. They got 0:70 acre of the disputed CS plot 40 by amalnama and dakhila. This claim of the said defendants on the basis of amalnama/dakhila is false as those documents are forged. Rashik Lalor Mohadev had no saleable/transferable rights in the suit land. Said suit is still pending. 

 13. Defendant No.11, another person having no title to the suit land raised a tin-shed in 1981 with pacca plinth on 0.03 acre of the disputed land and constructed another structure in the middle of plot No. 40 described in schedule No. E and delineated in the sketch map attached and marked as Y of the plaint. 

 14. In collusion with defendant-2, said defendant being an employee of Dhaka Municipal Corporation managed to mutate his name under holding No. 5/6 Topkhana Road Defendant No.12 also being an employee of said corporation managed to have another holding number i.e. 6/5 Topkhana Road in his name without having title and possession therein. He has raised another CI sheet structure attached to the structure of defendant No-11 in the last part of 1982. 

 20. The miscellaneous case was heard by Mr.  M.S. Saiful Islam, Joint District Judge 3rd Court, Dhaka, who allowed the same by his order dated 11.03.08 and restored the suit to its original file and number by setting aside the decree ex-parte which is impugned before us. 

 21. During hearing of the instant revisional application a supplementary affidavit was filed on behalf of the petitioners bringing on records a number of documents, namely, certified copy of the judgment passed in Title Suit No. 550 of 1984 filed by one A. Malek Howlader & others against the government. and others (Annexure-G) in which another Title Suit i.e., Title Suit .No. 551 of 1984 was also disposed of; certified copy of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 550 of 1984 (Annexure-G-1); certified copy of the common judgment and decree passed in Title Appeal Nos. 52 and 53 of 1985 preferred by the government against the judgment and decrees passed in aforesaid two suits (Annexure-H); appellate decree (Annexure-H-1); certified copy of the judgment passed in Civil Revision No. 531 and 532 of 1988 by a Single Bench of the High Court Division preferred by the government against the aforesaid appellate decrees (Annexure-1) and a judgment and order dated 12-3-1992 passed by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition No. 224 and 225 of 1991 filed at the instance of the government challenging the aforesaid judgment and order of the High Court Division (Annexure-1). 

 22. By all these documents what the present petitioners basically tried to show that the amalnama on the basis of which the present suit was filed was one upon which other persons claimed their respective title against the government and others in respect of some portions of the land of suit khatian and succeeded up to the Appellate Division. 

 23. A counter-affidavit was filed on behalf of the Government (OP-1) wherein it is stated, amongst other things, that the original suit was twice renumbered and the third time when the same was renumbered as Title Suit No. 113(G) of 1999 no notice was given to the government or its pleader. It was further stated that on 26-10-1998 was fixed for hearing of the suit but the plaintiff took adjournment. The next date was fixed on 24-11-1998 for final hearing but records were not produced before the Court on that date. Meanwhile the suit was transferred by the District Judge to another Court by his order dated 2-11-1998 of which no notice was received by the government. Thus keeping the government in dark a compromise decree was obtained practicing fraud upon Court. Learned judge, therefore, committed no illegality in allowing the miscellaneous case. 

 26. Learned Attorney General further pointed out that 5.18 acre land situated in the city centre, i.e., in Ramna Mouza and admittedly recorded in the khas khatian of the government. He apprised us that there are at least four important public buildings and installations situated in the suit land including old bungalows built during British period. The claimants of the entire invaluable property are mainly two persons of village Sreedharpur, Munshiganj posing to be sons of one late Gauranga Chandra Das so-called original plaintiff by virtue of an unregistered amalnama of 1339 BS which did not work out on account of series of mistakes and finally rested in a dakhila allegedly granted by GC Basak. In view of the peculiarities, he contended, the suit itself is meritless, frivolous and not maintainable. If the government is not given a chance to contest the suit multiplicity of litigation will follow. 

 "10. That it is stated that title suit No. 42 of 1988 was transferred vide administrative order of the learned District Judge, as such, no notice is required to be served upon either parties of the suit..." 

 30. Be that as it may, the instant suit is found to be transferred and renumbered as Title Suit No. 113(G) of 1999, which, as the learned Attorney General rightly pointed out, is a peculiar number which finally ended in decree on compromise as against some and ex-parte as against the government. The facts around transfer made for whatever reasons is unclear and the ignorance pleaded by the government is fairly justifiable. 

 33. Decree ex parte is passed in a manner as if absence of defendant ipso facto confers title of the suit land upon the plaintiff. And the plaintiffs are absolved of their duty to discharge their onus to prove their own case. Routine "decree passed ex parte on account merely of absence of the defendant has never found favour with the superior Courts. In Bangladesh vs A. Wadud; 25 DLR (SC) 90, it is held: 

 47. In the instant case a vast tract of land in the central area of Dhaka city (Topkhana Road) measuring an area of 5.18 acre (five acres and eighteen decimal) is claimed by two persons from a village of Munshiganj district on the basis of a Zamindari dakhila of 1944 as against record of rights admittedly standing in the name of the government and admitted possession of the Government at least from 1975, let alone, by construction of five public buildings thereon as claimed by the learned Attorney General as well as admitted possession of a good number of private defendants by virtue of decrees of law Courts and various registered and other title documents. 

 50. We have closely gone through supplementary affidavit filed on behalf of the petitioners and the judgment and decree Annexed thereto passed in Title Suit Nos. 550 and 551 of 1984 (analogously tried) obtained by one Abdul Malek Howlader & others and one Syed Md. Hanif and others respectively allegedly on the basis of the common amalnama upon which the plaintiff petitioner sought to place heavy reliance. Firstly, every suit has its own peculiar merit. The suit brought by the plaintiff must stand on its own merit. Furthermore, decree passed in some other suit brought by independent and separate individuals allegedly on the selfsame amalnama, even if true, is of no avail for the petitioner for the precise reason that the amalnama sought to be relied upon by the petitioner admittedly trailed away by series of mistakes affecting area and description of land sought to be settled with the plaintiffs predecessor and finally their title, as pleaded, rested on a dakhila issued by the original owner to effect the settlement. The amalnama, therefore was relegated to a vanishing point forming no more basis of the title of the plaintiffs. The factum that the Government lost up to the Appellate Division in those suits is not correct in the sense it is sought to be portrayed. Both the High Court Division and the Appellate Division dismissed the appeals by the government exclusively on limitation ground not on merit. Over and above the amalnama relied upon in those suits does not tally in material particulars with the amalnama used in the instant suit. 

 51. Order VII, rule 11 of the Code says, inter alia, that- 'the plaint shall be rejected where it does not disclose any cause of action'. 'Cause of action' is nowhere defined in the Code. Nonetheless, it is viewed by the superior Courts as the 'bundle of essential facts which is necessary for the plaintiff to prove before he can succeed in the suit.' It not only includes the facts necessary to support the plaintiff's title but also the facts which entitle him to relief against a particular defendant. 'Cause of action' as is held in Barikara Narasayya vs R. Basavana reported in (1985) 2 Civ LJ 649, ' means all that bundle of facts which would be necessary for the plaintiff to prove, if traversed, in order to support his right to the judgment of the Court' . 

 52. In the instant suit no 'cause of action' appears to have been disclosed so as to support the plaintiff's right to the judgment they ask for. The piece of an olden dakhila of 1944 which remains to be the sole basis of the title of the plaintiffs, even if proved on oath, cannot stand the test of credibility after so long years. The piece of dakhila even if taken to be true does not outweigh the preponderance of probabilities weighing in favour of the Government and other private defendants who are admittedly in possession of the suit land for decades by virtue of their continuous possession and title documents like registered deeds. A piece of private dakhila allegedly issued by an erstwhile Zamindar in 1944 can hardly, if ever, carry the suit through and finally bring success for the plaintiff. It is in the sense that the plaint does not disclose any 'cause of action' and the suit is virtually vexatious and meritless and the end result of the suit by the same token is clearly foreseeable. 

 Mere wishing to claim a property long occupied by the government under the claim of title and other individuals, if any, under the color of title on the basis of a scrap of paper representing a transactions between two or more private individuals long ago unsupported by any act of possession does not constitute cause of action and in that sense the suit would be barred under law, although strictly speaking, it may not be specifically barred by law."

parties:
Faizur Rahman and others ------ Appellants (in both the appeals)
Vs.
Abdul Hoque and others ------ Respondents (in both the appeals)
full_judgment:
2. The relevant facts are that the plaintiffs filed the suits being Title Suit No. 166 of 1976 for permanent injunction and Title Suit No. 97 of 1977 for declaration that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 92 of 1969, 4th Court of Munsif, Narayangonj, is illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiffs. 

 3. The plaintiffs in Title Suit No. 166 of 1976 claimed to have purchased the lands described in the schedule from the admit-ted owners on the basis of a decree passed in Title Suit No. 98 of 1967 by the Court of 2nd Munsif, Narayangonj, followed by execution of the required sale deed as well as delivery of possession through Title Execution Case No. 37 of 1967 and that thereafter one Nur Box sold his share to the plaintiff No. 6 by registered kabala dated 12.01.1970. Thus while the plaintiffs being owners as aforesaid were possessing the suit land detailed in schedule 'A' peacefully, the defendant Nos. 1-7 tried to dispossess the plaintiffs from the suit land claiming their title thereon on the basis of a decree dated 04.09.1974 passed in Title Suit No. 92 of 1969 and the sale deed obtained through Court on execution; of the said decree vide Execution Case No. 7 of 1975, which fact has been disclosed in the written objection and written statement filed by the defendants in Title Suit No. 166 of 1976 and faced with such situation the plaintiffs filed the Title Suit No. 97 of 1977 with prayer for declaring that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 92 of 1969 as illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiffs. In the plaint, of Title Suit No. 97 of 1977 the plaintiffs included schedules 'A' and 'B', of which schedule 'A' land corresponds to the schedule of P land detailed in the plaint of Title Suit No. 166 of 1976 and the lands detailed in schedule-B of Title Suit No. 97 of 1977 corresponds to the lands claimed by the defendants, got through execution of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 92 of 1969 vide Title Execution Case No. 7 of 1975. The respondents hereof as defendants contested both the suits by filing written statements. Both the parties adduced witnesses and produced documents, marked exhibits. 

 4. The contesting defendants of both the suits i.e. Title Suit No. 166 of 1976 and Title Suit No. 97 of 1977, as plaintiffs, filed Title Suit No. 92 of 1969 in the Court of 4th Munsif, Narayangonj, for Specific Performance of Contract, based on a sale-agreement dated 07.12.1963, wherein the plaintiffs of the instant suits were made defendants and they were contesting the suit (Title Suit No. 92 of 1969) and that the said suit was initially dismissed on 21.09.1971 for default. However after liberation of this Country they said suit was restored and ultimately heard and disposed of exparte on 04.09.1974 and the required kabala was obtained through Court by filing Execution Case No. 7 of 1975 covering the lands detailed in the schedule-land of the plaint of Title Suit No.166 of 1976, which is schedule-B land of Title Suit No.97 of 1977. 

 (2) Whether the plaintiffs are entitled to get decree as prayed for; 

 (3) Whether the plaintiffs are entitled to get a decree for permanent injunction as prayed for; and 

 (4) To what other relief(s) the plaintiffs are entitled to. 

 6. The learned Munsif heard both the cases together and recorded one set of depositions of witnesses for both the cases. On consideration of the materials and evidence available on record and the submissions of the learned Advocates of the respective parties learned Munsif decreed both the suits to the effect that the decree dated 04.09.1974 passed in Title Suit No.92 of 1969 by the 4th Court of made by the learned Advocates of the Munsif, Narayangonj, be declared as illegal, void, fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiffs and that the plaintiffs have acquired right, title and interest in schedule A land and that the defendant Nos.1-6 are permanently restrained, from entering into the schedule-A land. 

 7. Being aggrieved, the defendants preferred Title Appeal No. 223 of 1983 against the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 166 of 1976 and Title Appeal No. 224 of 1984 against the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 97 of 1977. The appeals were heard one after another and disposed of by a common judgment dated 19.03.1983 dismissing both the appeals holding, amongst others, that the plaintiffs were aware about the Title Suit No. 92 of 1969 and that the plaintiffs were found to be in possession of the suit land. 

 8. Being aggrieved there against the Civil Revision Cases were filed by the defendants in the High Court Division. The Civil Revision No. 761 of 1989 arose out of the judgment and decree passed in Title Appeal No. 224 of 1983 and Civil Revision No. 762 of 1989 arose out of Title Appeal No. 223 of 1983, which were heard one after another and disposed of by the common judgment and order dated 26.08.1999 making both the rules absolute, against which the present appeals were preferred upon obtaining leave. 

 10. We have considered the submissions respective parties. On careful examination of the submissions of the learner Advocates as well as the schedules 'A' 'B', as detailed and or referred to in IV plaints of the Title Suit No. 166 of 1976 Title Suit No. 97 of 1977 and Title Suit No. 92 of 1969, it appeared that out of the plots of land mentioned in the schedule of the plaints, except one plot; other plot are not same. But on the incorrect statement made in the written objection as well as in the written statement filed by the defendants in Title Suit No.166 of 1976 the plaintiffs had to file Title Suit No. 97 1977 for declaring that the judgment as decree dated 04.09.1974 passed in Tit Suit No.92 of 1969 by the Munsif, 4th Court, Narayangonj, as illegal, void fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiffs. 

 11. On consideration of the evidence are materials on record of the cases, appeared that the plaintiffs could not prove their claim that they were not away about the exparte decree passed in Title Suit No. 92 of 1969 in the year 1974, rather it is found from the copy of the order sheet of Title Suit No. 92 of 1969, annexed to the Additional Paper Boo filed on 12.04.2009 by the Appellants, the after liberation of the Country on restoration of the suit (Title Suit No. 92 of 1969 to its original file and number, since d missed for default earlier, the defender, appeared in the suit on 19.04.1972, 18.07.1972 and 18.12.1973 but did not appear at the hearing and the suit w decreed exparte on 04.09.1974. 

 12. It appears on comparison of the land described in the schedule of the plaintiff Title Suit No. 92 of 1969 and the lands described in the schedules of plaint of 'We Suit No. 97 and 1977 that the scheduled lands of Title Suit No. 92 of 1969 do of correspond to the lands detailed in Schedule-B of the plaint of Title Suit No. 97 of 1977 and those are not same or Common, except one plot being plot N0.158 under Khatian No. 51 measuring 15 decimals as to the lands detailed in Schedule of Title Suit No. 166 of 1976 and Schedule-A of Title Suit No. 97 of 1977. 

 13. The plaintiffs of Title Suit No. 97 of 1977 and Title Suit No. 166 of 1976 aimed, to have purchased land measuring 1.58 acres in four plots detailed in schedule-A of the plaint of Title Suit No. 97 of 1977 and in the schedule of Title Suit No. 166 of 1976, which are as under:- 

 14. The lands described in schedule of the plaint of Title Suit No.92 of 1969 are detailed in Schedule-B of the plaint of the Title Suit No.97 of 1977 which are as Under: 

 16. Thus there could not be any cause of action for challenging the decree passed in Title Suit No. 92 of 1969 by the plaintiffs and that the defendants having no claim for any right, title and interest in respect of other three plots of Schedule-A land i.e. plot Nos. 121, 159 and 119 the plaintiffs may get a decree for permanent injunction as prayed for in Title Suit No.166 of 1976 against the defendants in respect of the lands detailed in Schedule-A, except said plot No. 168 under Khatian No. 51 admeasuring 15 decimals, which is described as a pond/ditch, which plot appears to be included in the schedules of both Title Suit No. 92 of 1969 and Title Suit No. 166 of 1976 and that the dispute relating to Plot No. 168 under Khatian No. 51 may be resolved separately, if the parties so desire, in a proper forum and in accordance with law. 

 17. Thus, we are of the view that the plain-tiff-appellants may get a decree for permanent injunction in Title Suit No.166 of 1976 in respect of the Schedule-A lands except said 15 decimals of land being a pond in plot No. 168 under Khatian No. 51 restraining the defendants from interfering illegally or forcibly with the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs thereon. The Title Suit No. 97 of 1977 is liable to be dismissed being barred by limitation, since the record of the Title Suit No. 92 of 1969 shows that the plaintiffs hereof, being defendants in Title Suit No. 92 of 1969, took steps in the suit after its restoration after liberation of the Country in 1972 and thus aware about the decree passed in Title Suit No. 92 of 1969 in the year 1974 and also for want of cause of action having no proof of any right, title or interest on the lands in reference. 

 18. Accordingly the Civil Appeal No. 229 of 2002 is dismissed with cost and the Civil Appeal No. 230 of 2002 is allowed in part but without any order as to costs. Thus Title Suit No. 97 of 1977 is dismissed and the Title Suit No. 166 of 1976 is decreed in part. The defendant Nos.1-6 are accordingly restrained permanently from entering into and or interfering with peaceful possession of the plaintiffs in the land detailed in the schedule of the plaint of Title Suit No. 166 of 1976, except Plot No.168 under Khatian No.15 measuring 15 decimals of land. The lands on which injunction in granted, are situated within the District-Dhaka, P.S. Fatullah, Mouja No.152 Pikuni, consisting of 39 decimals (Nal) in Plot No. 121 on the North of which is Audhar Mondal and 56 decimals (Nal) in Plot No. 159 on the North which is Halat and both plots are and Khatian No. 161; and 48 decimals (Nal) Plot No. 119 on the North of which Makhan Mondal under Khatil Nos. 173/189/20 and the total area land which is 1.43 acres.

full_judgment:
2. The petitioner as plaintiff brought Title suit No. 370 of 1982 in the court of first Munsif, Noakhali against the opposite parties and others for the declaration of their right and title in the suit land described in the schedule of the plaint stating, inter alia, that they are the owners in possession of the suit land by way of settlement from the original zamindar upon executing a registered kabuliyat dated 24.11.1943 and since then, they have been owning and possessing the same on payment of taxes; that the wrong recording of Diara khatian in name of the three sets of defendants opposite parties in different khatians have not created any right, title, interest and possession in the suit land which cast a cloud on their title and hence the suit. 

 3. The defendant having been duly served the notice of summons neither appeared nor contested the suit whereupon the learned Munsif after several adjournments passed an exparte decree dated 29.12.1982 in title Suit No. 370 of 1982. 

 4. On 15.03.1983 the opposite parties as petitioner brought miscellaneous case No. 25 of 1983 under order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the 1st court of Munsif, Noakhali for the restoration of the Title Suit No. 370 of 1982 to its original file and number after setting aside the exparte decree dated 29.12.1982 as the same was obtained collusively upon suppression of summons and copies of plaint to them; that on 13.03.1983 knowing about the exparte decree at Tahashil office of Miar Hat and became definite of it on 14.03.1983 after searching for the same at Maijdee. 

 5. Petitioner having appeared contested the case by filing a written objection denying the material allegation contained therein stating inter alia that all that have been stated in the application under order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure are all false, concocted, motivated and without any basis; that the summons and copies of the plaint were duly served upon them by the process server in accordance with law before so many witnesses; that they had full knowledge about the institution of the Title Suit No. 370 of 1982 and deliberately and intentionally stayed out of taking any steps knowing fully well that it would be of no use of contesting the suit and the present miscellaneous case is brought only to harass the petitioners at the instigation of some touts and as such the same being a vexatious and frivolous litigation is liable to be discharged. 

 9. Mr. Nikalesh Dutta, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that in order to prove the service of summons and copies of plaint two PWs and 3 DWs including OPW 3 Abul Kashem who was a Process Server was examined who categorically deposed that service of summons was properly served upon the defendants by hanging before the witnesses on their refusal to accept the same and Shamsul Hoque as DW-3 was examined as a witness who was present and signed during the service of summons. He further submits that there had been service of summons and copies of plaint on the defendants in the original suit in accordance with law and the opposite parties have miserably failed to prove their own contention of suppression of summons and that the learned Assistant Judge having arrived at the positive finding that the Miscellaneous case is barred by limitation. He further submits that the learned Assistant Judge erred in law resulting an error in the decision causing failure of justice in allowing the Miscellaneous case. 

 12. Now the point for determination is whether the learned Assistant Judge, Sadar Upazilla Noakhali committed any illegality and material irregularity in passing the impugned judgment and order dated 23.08.1988 and whether the plaintiff petitioners are entitled to get any relief in this revision. 

 17. The main point for determination is whether the summons have been duly served upon the defendants of the original suit. The finding of the trial court is that the summons were served under order 5 Rule 17 of the CPC. After giving such kind of finding, it is strange how he has passed the impugned order. 

 19. The learned Assistant Judge has made a self contradictory finding on vital points. Thus he erred in law in contradicting himself and thus he erred in law resulting a error in his decisions causing failure of justice in allowing the Miscellaneous case for restoration as required under the provisions of order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil procedure. There being iota of evidence or materials on record that there has been suppression of summons or that summons have not been served on them in accordance with law. The learned Assistant Judge in order to allow the miscellaneous case under order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure without an order for restoration of the original suit to its file and number is bad in law resulting a failure of justice. 

 20. Suit being declaration of wrong recording of khatians recorded in respect of three sets of defendants separately out of which one set of defendants having compromised his interest in Title suit No. 172 of 1983, the learned Assistant Judge erred in law resulting an error in decisions in allowing the miscellaneous case for restoration causing failure of justice inasmuch as the opening of the suit would re-open the matter already compromised. 

 25. Hence the plaintiff petitioner is entitled to get relief as prayed for.
