full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: The appeal, by leave, at the instance of the defendants is against the judgment dated August 10,1997 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Second Appeal No. 162 of 1975 dismissing the same upon affirming the judgment and decree dated April 20, 1974 of the Court of Additional District Judge, Rangpur in Other Appeal No. 175 of 1970 allowing the same upon setting aside the judgment and decree dated June 23, 1970 of the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) Rangpur in Other Suit No. 45 of 1968 so far the same relates to the land described in schedule 'Kha' and 'Ga' of the plaint. The aforementioned suit was filed seeking declaration of title in respect of the land of schedule 'Ka' of Mouza Son a-tala and as regard the land of schedule 'Kha and 'Ga' of Mouza Sandalpur. 

 4. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 4, 11, 12 and 13 by filing joint written statement stating, inter alia, that Izzatullah Chowdhury purchased the land of 'Ka' schedule in a rent sale in the benami of plaintiff No. 2, wife of Tofazzal Hossain (since deceased) who was foster son of Izzatullah Chowdhury, that lzzatullah Chowdhury was the real owner of the property, described in schedule 'Kha' and 'Ga' and he created a benami deed in respect of the land of said 2 schedules in the name of his foster son Tofazzal Hossain in fear of Marwari creditors, that the sale in favour of Tofazzal Hossain in respect of the land of 'Kha' and Ga' schedule was never acted upon, nor it was treated as a deed of transfer by any of the parties to the deed, that Izzatullah Chowdhury during his lifetime was in possession of all the disputed property through bargaders, that plaintiff No. 2 while staying in the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury as widow of his foster son, Tofazzal Hossain, fraudulently obtained possession of some original documents including the deed dated 25 Falgoon, 1345 BS, and transferred those documents to her father's house, that Izzatullah Chowdhury having had come to know of the said fact drove away Khatemon from his house about a year before his death. 

 5. The trial Court on consideration of the materials on record relating to 'Ka' schedule land i.e. plaintiffs' case of purchasing the land of said schedule by plaintiff No. 2 and the case of the contesting defendants as to purchasing the 'Ka' schedule by Izzatullah Chowdhury in the benami of plaintiff No.2 held that plaintiff No.2 is the real owner of the land in 'Ka' schedule. The trial Court while considering the case of the plaintiffs and the defendants as regard the land of' Kha' and 'Ga' schedule observed that question of possession of the property will not be of very much help to ascertain the real title of the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule. In the background of the admitted circumstances that Tofazzal Hossain till his death in 1353 BS with his wife Khatemon lived in the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury and after death of Tofazzal his wife Khatemon lived in the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury with children and, as such, "it is very difficult to distinguish the possession of Khatemon from that of Izzatullah Chowdhury", that question of inadequate consideration will not be a sufficient ground for taking the view that the transaction was a benami transfer since the transfer in question by Exhibit-l was made by a foster father in favour of his foster son, that passing of consideration as deposed by the scribe of Exhibit-1 in the proceeding under section 145 CrPC being of a professional deed writer in the absence of other independent witness cannot be relied upon safely and, as such, the matter or passing of consideration "does not help us much in determining the real dispute as to title", that the question of custody of the original document with plaintiff No.2 "does not help me very much in determining the real title" since from the evidence on record it is seen that PW 2's position in the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury "was that of a mistress" so long she was there and in that state of the matter it is quite probable that she took Exhibit-l in her custody and for which trouble started between her and lzzatullah Chowdhury and finally, she was driven out with her children from the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury, that the motive for making benami transaction by Exhibit-1 could not be established since lzzatullah Chowdhury "had no substantial debt to justify a Benami transaction for fear of any Marwari creditor", that in the background of dealing with the property of Exhibit-l i.e. property of khatian Nos. 28 and 47, by Izzatullah Chowdhury by the Exhibit- A dated 13-1-1944 and dealing with the property that Tofazzal's sister Amena Khatun got from lzzatullah Chowdhury by Exhibit-A and dealing with the said property as reflected by Exhibit-A(1) and Exhibit-A(2) clearly indicates that IzzatuJlah Chowdhury "did never intend to make any bonafide transfer by the earlier kabala Exhibitl in favour of his foster son Tofazzal Hossain", that the subsequent transfers by the kabalas Exhibits A(1) and A (2) are bonafide trans- fers, that Izzatullah Chowdhury transferred the land of khatian Nos. 28 and 47 by Exhibit-A to Tofazzal's sister Amena to his knowledge and that transfer made by Izzatullah Chowdhury to Tofazzal's sister Amena was a bonafide transfer, that from the rent decree Exhibit- 3(b) it cannot be said that the said rent suit was in respect of the land of khatian No. 31, that there is gulf of difference between the rent decree (Exhibit- 3(b) and the transfer made by the kabala Exhibit-A, that the Exhibit-A reveals the con-duct of Izzatullah Chowdhury and Tofazzal Hossain who are parties to the kabala, Exhibit-l but the Exhibit-3 reveals the conduct of the heirs of Tofazzal Hossain after his death and that it is also not known what was the nature of the ex parte rent decree, that discrepancies in the body of the kabala and the schedule thereof (Exhibit-1) sufficiently indicates that lzzatullah Chowdhury "made no bonafide transfer by the kabala Exhibit-1 ", since a vendor always takes reasonable care as regard the land he transferred when the same is a real one, that Exhibit-B series dakhilas as regard the land of Sandalpur, the lands in dispute are in the name of Izzatullah Chowdhury and the same are "more dependable than the dakhilas produced by the plaintiffs in their names", that in the facts and circumstances of the case it can reasonably be held that Izzatullah Chowdhury never intended to make "any bonafide and real transfer by the kabala Exhibit-1 in favour of his foster son Tofazzal Hossain." On the aforesaid findings and decisions the trial Court held that "neither Tofazzal nor the plaintiffs acquired any bonafide title in the disputed lands of Kha and Ga Schedule." As stated hereinbefore the trial Court decreed the suit in respect of the land of 'Ka' schedule but dismissed the suit in respect of the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule. 

 6. The plaintiffs as against the part of the judgment and decree of the trial Court i.e. dismissing the plaintiffs' suit in respect of the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule, went on appeal. From the defendants' side there was no appeal as against the judgment and decree of the trial Court decreeing the suit in respect of the land of Ka' schedule. The appellate Court set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court so far the same related to the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule on the findings that in the background of the materials on record, particularly evidence as to payment of consideration by Tofazzal Hossain in connection with Exhibit-1, the trial Court should have held that Exhibit-l is a valid document and the same was duly acted upon, that the trial Court, upon taking into consideration transaction made by Exhibit A, was in error in holding that Exhibit-I was not a bonafide deed of transfer and that it was not acted upon, that taking into consideration the fact that Exhibit-I was registered on 25th Falgoon, 1345 BS and Tofazzal Hossain married PW 2 in Baishakh, 1346 BS the contention of the plaintiffs that Exhibit- 1 was made for making provision for the future of TofazzaI cannot be lightly brushed aside, since in the background of the admitted position that Tofazzal Hossain and his wife, plaintiff No.2 stayed in the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury, that plaintiffs having had established by oral and documentary evidence that Tofazzal Hossain and after his death his heirs possessed the land of Exhibit-1 and the said fact clearly established the fact that by Exhibit-1 Tofazzal acquired title in the land of schedule 'Kha'' and 'Ga', that Exhibit-3(a), the certified copy of the rent decree, also shows that Tofazzal Hossain exercised his right and title in respect of the land of khatian No. 28 i.e. land of the 'Kha' schedule, that evidence of DW 2 proves the possession of the land in suit by the plaintiffs through bargader, that plaintiffs have succeeded in establishing that Tofazzal Hossain exclusively possessed the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule and the fact of possession of the land goes long way in determining the real nature of Exhibit-1, that because of the relationship between the vendor and vendee low price, as in the case of Exhibit-I cannot be the ground for holding that the transaction was a benami one, that payment of consideration money as regard the transaction made by the Exhibit-I has been proved by Exhibit- 8, the deposition of the scribe, that the trial Court was not well founded to discard the evidence of the scribe on the view that evidence of the scribe of Exhibit-I was of a professional deed writer since "deed writers under all circumstances do not depose falsely", that contention of the defendants that plaintiff No. 2 for illegal gain took away the Exhibit-l is nothing but a device "to nullify the effect of evidentiary value regarding custody of original document", that from the evidence of DWs it is seen that Izzatullah Chowdhury had no substantial debt upon borrowing from Marwari and, as such, the contention of the defendants that to put away the property or Exhibit-1 from the clutch of the creditor Izzatullah Chowdhury made Exhibit-1 is of no merit, that taking into consideration the fact of payment of consideration money by Tofazzal for the transaction evidenced by Exhibit-1 and possession of the land of Exhibit-1 by Tofazzal Hossain and after him his heirs and payment of rent to the Zamindar as well as to the Government by Tofazzal Hossain and his heirs and failure on the part of the defendants to prove that Exhibit-1 is a benami document, the only conclusion is that "kabala (Exhibit-1) is a bonafide, valid and active document. In fact, it operated to pass title in favour of Tofazzal," that presence of Tofazzal Hossain in the office of sub-Registrar on the date when by Exhibit-A, Izzatullah Chowdhury transferred 2.40½ acres of land of Exhibit-1 to. Tofazzal's sister, Arnena and by Exhibit-1 (a) Amena transferred land to her brother Tofazzal does not saddle Tofazzal Hossain with the knowledge of the transfer of land of Exhibit-1 by Izzatullah Chowdhury by the Exhibit-A to Amena, sister of Tofazzal Hossain, that the transaction made by Izzatullah Chowdhury by Exhibit-A and the transaction made by Amena by Exhibit-A(1) did not affect the validity of Exhibit-1 since the same has been found "a valid and bonafide document and title of the disputed land passed by it", that Exhibit-A executed by Izzatullah Chowdhury as regard the land of khatian Nos. 28 and 47 i.e. land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule, "cannot nullify the effect of Exhibit-1 ", that there is nothing on the record to show what prompted Izzatullah Chowdhury to make sham transaction by Exhibit-1 , that when motive for making benami transaction by Exhibit-1 could not be proved by the defendants and it having been established that Izzatullah Chowdhury for the future provision of Tofazzal Hossain made Exhibit-1, as such "it can be reasonably presumed that transaction witnessed by Exhibit-1 is a bonafide and real one", that the conclusion so made gets supported from the subsequent transfer made by Izzatullah Chowdhury to plaintiff No. 2's son, plaintiff No. 4 by Exhibit-4, that in the context of the fact on record it cannot be said that Exhibit-I was not acted upon, that in the background of the consideration of the facts and the circumstance, only conclusion that can be derived is Exhibit-1" is a valid and active document and Tofazzal acquired valid title to the land of schedule Kha and Ga by virtue of that deed" and, as such, plaintiffs have right, title and possession in the land of 'Kha' and 'Ga' schedule. 

 12. The learned Counsel of the plaintiff-respondents submitted that the lower appellate Court on detailed discussions of the materials on record arrived at the finding that the document, Exhibit-I was genuine and bonafide and the said finding of the lower appellate Court having been upheld by the High Court Division, the said finding of fact sparingly interfered by the superior Court unless the finding is against the materials on record or in arriving at the said finding there was procedural error of law or that the finding arrived at was based on misconstruction of a document and misreading of the materials on record. The learned Counsel also submitted that none of the aforesaid situations being not present in respect of the finding arrived at by the lower appellate Court and affirmed by the High Court Division there is no occasion for interfering with the judgment under appeal. It has further been submitted by the learned Counsel since the Exhibit- 1 is a genuine and bonafide document and there being no provision in the same for revocation on the intervention of certain factor and, as such, even if there had been transfer by Izzatullah Chowdhury by the Exhibit-A for that there was no revocation of Exhibit-1 and, as such, the right, title and interest of Tofazzal Hossain having not been affected by the act of Izzatullah Chowdhury by Exhibit-A, the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs is very much in the land in suit as being the heirs of Tofazzal Hossain in whose favour right and title in the land in suit accrued on the basis of Exhibit-1. 

 13. The learned Counsel continued that, upon taking into consideration Exhibit-A and the transactions of the land acquired by Exhibit-A by recipient of Exhibit-A there cannot be a conclusion that document Exhibit-1 was a benami transaction, that transaction made by Izzatullah Chowdhury by the Exhibit-A was hit by the provision of section 53 of the Transfer of Property Act (the Act) as well as by the provision of section 42 of the Act and that there has been an attempt on the part of Izzatullah Chowdhury to defraud Tofazzal Hossain by the Exhibit-A, that lower appellate Court as well as High Court Division having had considered all the accepted ingredients of benami transaction and' having .had found absent in respect of the transaction made by Izzatullah Chowdhury by Exhibit-1 the finding of the said Courts that the transfer made by Izzatullah Chowdhury by Exhibit-1 to Tofazzal Hossain was an out and out sale and that was not a benami transfer and as there has been no error of law by the lower appellate Court as well as by the High Court Division in arriving at the aforesaid finding i.e. the Exhibit-1 is a complete sale deed and thereby created right in respect of the land so transferred in favour of Tofazzal Hossain, no interference is called for with judgment of the High Court Division. The learned Counsel in continuation of the submission that Exhibit I is not a benami transaction has referred to the finding of the lower appellate Court that consideration money in respect of the transaction took place by Exhibit-1 was paid by Tofazzal Hossain that, the Exhibit-1 has been produced from the custody of plaintiff No. 2, that land transferred by the Exhibit-1 was possessed by Tofazzal Hossain in exercise of his independent right in presence of Izzatullah Chowdhury and rent was paid by Tofazzal Hossain and after his death his heirs and thus taking the aforesaid facts along with the fact that the defendants failed to prove that Exhibit-l was a benami document, there could be only one conclusion that Exhibit-A is a bonafide, valid and active document and that by the same title passed to Tofazzal Hossain. It has also been submitted by the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-respondents since Exhibit-1 is a valid and bona- fide document and the title passed by the said document the subsequent transfer by Exhibit-A of the land of Exhibit-1 did not affect the validity of the Exhibit-1. 

 20. The learned Counsel for the appellant in support of his contention that Exhibit-1 was a benami document emphasised the subsequent conduct of the maker of the document i.e. Izzatullah Chowdhury, as demonstrated by Exhibit-A and in support of the aforesaid contention, i.e. subsequent conduct of the maker of the document which is being claimed as benami document, is material in determining the nature and character of the said document, has referred to the case of Nurjahan Begum vs Mahmudur Rahman Mallick reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 506 (same case has also been reported in 34 DLR (AD) 61). Therein it has been observed "but their subsequent conduct including their dealings and the enjoyment of the property become relevant factors for consideration". In the aforesaid case, it has also been observed : "In a benami transaction source of purchase money is an important criteria but it is not conclusive …..Source of consideration money though an important criteria in a benami transaction, but in the absence of an unambiguous ownership consideration of other relevant circumstances become important in a case where ownership is disputed. The disputed question of benami cannot be determined only on the consideration of source of consideration money, and it becomes incumbent for the court to fall back upon the surrounding circumstances of the transaction, the position of the parties and the relationship to each other". The learned Counsel for the appellants has submitted that the High Court Division as well as the lower appellate Court in determining the nature of Exhibit-l in the negative or, in other words, Exhibit-l is not a benami document but sale deed, did not at all give any importance relating to the subsequent conduct of the parties i.e. transfer of the property of Exhibit-1 by Izzatullah Chowdhury in the year 1944 by Exhibit-A to Amena, sister of Tofazzal Hossain. The learned Counsel as regard the matter of intention of the parties to the document Exhibit-1, upon emphasising the fact of transfer made by lzzatullah Chowdhury by the Exhibit-A. submitted had Izzatullah Chowdhury intended to transfer title of the property as are "in Exhibit-I to Tofazzal Hossain in that case he would not have dealt with the property later on by Exhibit-A. The learned Counsel also referred to case of Bhim Singh (dead) by LRs vs Kan Singh reported in AIR 1980 (SC) 727 wherein following observation has been made: "The second case which is loosely termed as a benami transaction is a case whether a person who is the owner of the property executes a conveyance in favour of another without the intention of transferring the title to the property there under. In this case, the transferor continues to be the real owner". It is the contention of the learned Counsel for the appellants since the Exhibit-A clearly demonstrates that Izzatullah Chowdhury had never intended to transfer the land as are in Exhibit-l to Tofazzal Hossain and, as such, the High Court Division as well as the Court of appeal below were in serious error in holding that by Exhibit-1 Tofazzal acquired title without taking into consideration the material fact as demonstrated by Exhibit-A that Izzatullah Chowdhury never intended to transfer title of the land as in Exhibit-l to Tofazzal Hossain. 

 22. Though amongst other circumstances possession of the property, which is claimed to have been acquired in a benami transaction or that the transaction which is claimed to be benami, is considered important and also relevant, but in the instant case in the background of the fact i.e. Tofazzal Hossain had no separate identity being foster son of Izzatullah Chowdhury and after marriage Tofazzal Hossain and his wife and their children stayed with Izzatullah Chowdhury and after death of Tofazzal Hossain in 1353 BS his wife and children stayed with Izzatullah Chowdhury upto Kartick, 1366 BS when Tofazzal's wife and children were driven away by Izzatullah Chowdhury. As it is the undenied position that Tofazzal's wife and his children stayed with Izzatullah Chowdhury till they were driven out from the house of Izzatullah Chowdhury, it, with certainty and definiteness, cannot be said that possession of the property of Exhibit-1 by Tofazzal Hossain and after him by his wife and children was distinguishable from the possession which Izzatullah Chowdhury had in the property in question as well as other property. In deciding the question of benami amongst other circumstances the fact of subsequent dealing with the property of the transaction which is being claimed to be benami is also considered important. In the instant case it is seen that after execution and registration of Exhibit-1 by Izzatullah Chowdhury in 1939 in favour of Tofazzal Hossain in the year 1944 some property of the said Exhibit-1 was transferred by Izzatullah Chowdhury in favour of Tofazzal's sister and this shows the intention of Izzatullah Chowdhury as regard the transaction made by Exhibit-L Had Izzatullah Chowdhury in, fact transferred the property vesting title in Tofazzal Hossain by Exhibit-I then certainly he would not have gone for dealing with the property of Exhibit- 1 subsequently by alienation by Exhibit- A to Amena, sister of Tofazzal Hossain. It may also be mentioned whatever property was acquired by Amena by Exhibit-A, she transferred some thereof  by Exhibits A(1) and A(2). The transaction made by Izzatullah Chowdhury by Exhibit-A clearly shows that he never intended to vest any title of the property of Exhibit-I with Tofazzal Hossain. It may be mentioned that on the date of transaction by Exhibit-A by Izzatullah Chowdhury, Tofazzal Hossain was very much in the office of Sub-Registrar and this shows that transaction by Exhibit-A was made to the knowledge of Tofazzal Hossain and thus conclusion can logically be derived that Tofazzal Hossain was quite certain that by Exhibit-1 no title was vested in him in respect of the property of the said document. In deciding the question of benami intention of the owner of the property executing a conveyance in favour of another whether intended to transfer the title to the property thereby is considered a factor. It has already been seen that subsequent dealing with the property by the Exhibit- A by Izzatullah Chowdhury clearly establishes the fact that he never intended to transfer the title as regard the property of Exhibit-I to Tofazzal. In the background of the afore state of the matter, it can be said that transaction that was made by Exhibit-1 was a benami transaction.

parties:
M.A. Aziz.  ------ Petitioner.
Vs.
Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Housing and Public Works, Bangladesh Secretariat, Ramna, Dhaka and another.  ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
2. Short fact of the case is that the respondent No. 1 as the plaintiff filed the Title Suit No. 172 of 2000 in the Court of The Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka alleging, inter-alia, that decree passed on 14.08.1972 in Title Suit No. 64 of the Court of First Subordinate Judge, Dhaka was obtained by practising fraud and forgery upon the Court by the defendant No. 1 and as such the same is void and not binding on the Government for a declaration that the judgment dated 10.04.1997 passed in Writ Petition No. 2456 of 1996 and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 744 of 1997 on the basis of the aforesaid decree in Title Suit No. 64 of 1972 were also obtained by practising fraud and forgery on the Court and are therefore inoperative, null and void and have no legal force and as such not binding upon the plaintiff and for a further declaration that the schedule No. 1 property was not the subject matter of the solenama decree in the Title Suit No. 64 of 1972 a decree for permanent injunction restraining the defendant No. 1 from claiming or demanding or interfering with and /or disturbing the possession of the plaintiff in schedule No,  property and to award cost of the suit and to pass such other and further order or orders as court may deem fit and proper as per law and equity. 

 4. Defendant No. 1 appeared in the Transfer Petition No. 2 of 2000 and filed an application for discharging the Rule stating, inter-alia, that the Title Suit No. 172 of 2000 was fixed on 11.09.2002 for steps of the plaintiff but the plaintiff failed to take necessary steps whereupon the Joint District Judge fixed 14.11.2002 for steps of the plaintiff and on that date the plaintiff filed an application for adjournment to take steps. Thereafter, the plaintiff again failed to take necessary steps on the fixed dates and the suit was dismissed for default on 22.04.2003. The plaintiff of the Title Suit No. 172 of 2000 filed and application on 27.10.2003 under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the trial. Court for restoration of the said Title Suit No. 172 of 2000 and upon hearing the plaintiff-petitioner, the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka rejected the application for restoration by his order No. 15 dated 06.11.2003. Thereafter, the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 172 of 2000 filed a Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 2003 under order 9 Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 11.11.2003 for restoration of the aforesaid title suit, which is still pending in the Court of Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka and the Miscellaneous Case was fixed on 20.01.2004 for filing written objection by the respondent No. 1. The respondent No.1 filled an application for calling for the record of Title Suit No. 172 of 2000 by suppressing the fact that the suit was not pending in the lower Court, upon hearing the learned Advocate of the respondent the Bench consisting of Mr. Justice Amirul kabir Chowdhury and Mr. Justice Syed A. B. Mahmudul Haque were pleased to call for the record though there was no such suit pending in the lower Court. Actually when the title suit was dismissed for default on 22.04.2003 the present rule automatically became infructuous. The respondent filed this transfer petition for withdrawal of Title Suit No. 172 of 2000 which was pending in the Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka and during pendency of the present rule the title suit was dis-missed for default on 22.04.2003 and the Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 2003 for restoration is still pending and as such the present rule has become infractuous as it is the mandatory provision of Article 110 of the Constitution that a suit must be pending in the lower Court which is to be withdrawn. Since Title Suit No. 172 of 2000 is not pending in the Court of 3rd Joint District Judge, Dhaka there is no question of withdrawal of that suit for disposal by the High Court Division and as such the instant rule became infractuous. 

 5. Thereafter, the plaintiff-respondent filed an application for hearing of the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 2003 arising out of Title Suit No. 172 of 2000 now pending in the Court of 3rd Joint Distract Judge, Dhaka. The High Court Division thereafter allowed the petition for hearing of the Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 2003 and fixed the matter for hearing. 

 8. Mr. Abdus Salam Khan, learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that it is an error apparent on the face of the judgment of the Appellate Division in that the Appellate Division manifestly failed to consider that the Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 2003 for restoration of Title Suit No. 172 of 2000 to its original file and number by setting aside the dismissal order dated 22.04.2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka is not a case as contemplated under Article 110 of the Constitution for disposal by the High Court Division and therefore, the High court Division acted without jurisdiction in allowing the hearing of the above Miscellaneous Case by itself which is not contemplated under Article 110 of the Constitution. He further submits that it is an error apparent on the face of the judgment of the Appellate Division that the said Division glaringly omitted to take notice of the fact that the Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 2003 was filed under order IX, Rule IV of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of Title Suit No. 172 of 2000 which was dismissed for default and the said Miscellaneous Case does not involve any substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution or any point of general public importance and, therefore, the High Court Division acted without jurisdiction and committed an error of law apparent on the face of record to allow the hearing of the said Miscellaneous Case by the High Court Division for restoration of the said Title Suit which was dismissed for default. He next submits that the Appellate Division erred in dismissing the case in the ends of justice and for the sake of complete justice, the appeal should have been allowed.

parties:
Zila Parishad, Chittagong ----- Petitioner 
Vs. 
Abdul Halim and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. Opposite party Nos. 1-8 instituted the suit for declaration of title by adverse possession in the suit property and for further declaration that the RS khatian and other corresponding khatians in respect of the suit lands were prepared in accordance with law. 

 3. Plaint case, in short, is that the suit lands along with other property belonged to Azmot Ali Khan Nayabad Taluk. Golam Gafur Sawdagor and Asgor Ali took settlement of the suit lands by registered deed dated 20th February, 1877. Previously the suit lands were used as tea garden but subsequently, the then Government gave possession of some lands in favour of Golam Gafur Sawdagor and thereafter, the Government took over possession of the remaining lands and handed over the same in favour of the Zila Parishad. Golam Gafur Sawdagor died leaving four sons, Kala Miah, Asmot Ali, Abdus Samad, Abdul Goni and daughters Ammajan and Mirujan. The lands were recorded in CS No. 130 kheyat khatian in their names. Kala Miah died unmarried and his other brother Abdul Gani got the suit lands exclusively by an amicable partition. Abdul Gani died before the preparation of the RS record and the lands were recorded in RS khatian No. 982 in the name of his son Noor Hossain. The defendant did not file any objection against the said record. Noor Hossain handed over possession of the said lands in favour of Moqbul Ahmed by deed dated 26th October 1944. Moqbul Ahmed thereafter transferred it in favour of Haji Fazor Rahman and Saleh Ahmed Sowdagor by kabala dated 14th April 1948. Saleh Ahmed thereafter by kabalas dated 2nd October 1954 and 12th October 1954 transferred his share in favour of Abdul Monaf Contractor. The RS record was also prepared in his name. Abdul Monaf developed the suit lands, raised semipucca structures thereon and rented the said houses to the tenants. A Municipality holding was prepared in the name of the plaintiffs' predecessor. After the death of Abdul Monaf Contractor, the plaintiffs inherited the suit lands. The further case of the plaintiffs is that though the Zila Parishad's right to realise rent from the plaintiffs was extinguished, it served a notice upon them which clouded their title in the suit lands. The plaintiffs failed to obtain proper reliefs in Other Class Suit No. 95 of 1992 as they sought irrelevant reliefs in that suit. The Zila Parishad gained over the tenants of the plaintiffs who denied the plaintiffs' title, for which, the plaintiffs were compelled to institute the suit. 

 4. The case of the defendant, in short, is that the plaintiffs have not acquired any title on the strength of deed dated 20th February 1877, that the said deed does not attract the suit lands and that without a local investigation it is not possible to ascertain whether the suit lands appertain to RS khatian No. 982. Its further case was that the RS record was wrongly prepared in the name of the plaintiffs predecessor. The suit lands belonged to the Zila Parishad under the Government. The plaintiff's predecessor in collusion with the corrupt staffs of the Zila Parishad got the suit lands recorded in his name in RS khatian No. 982 as possessor in the remark column. Zila Parishad did not settle the suit lands in favour of Noor Hossain. The plaintiffs instituted Other Class Suit No. 95 of 1992 in respect of the suit lands and they lost in First Appeal No. 39 of 1995 in the High Court Division, and in the Appellate Division and thus, the suit is hit by the principles of res judicata and therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 6. Mr Md Obaidur Rahman Mostafa, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, argues that admittedly the plaintiffs have failed to establish their title by adverse possessions in the suit lands up to the Appellate Division and that the Courts below on a misreading of the judgments, Exhibits B and B (1), have erroneously held that the suit was not barred by res judicata. In this connection, the learned Advocate has taken us to the plaints and the judgments. 

 7. On a plain reading of the plaint, we find inconsistent claim of the plaintiffs in the suit lands. Initially, they made averments in paragraph 1(one) of the plaint stating that "১নং বিবাদী ৮.২৮ একরের মধ্যে ৭.৭০ একর জমি নিজ খাস দখলে রাখিয়া ৫৮ শতক আব্দুল গনির পুত্র নুর হোসেন নামক ব্যক্তির বরাবরে ১১। ৩(১১ আনা তিন পাই) খাজনা ধার্য্যে লগিয়ত করেন” After institution of the suit, they filed an application for amendment of the plaint and the prayer was allowed on 11th May, 2002. In the said amendment they inserted one paragraph at the top as paragraph No. 1 one and the original paragraph No.1(one) has been numbered as 1(ka). By way of amendment, they have introduced a new story about the plaintiffs acquisition of title in the suit lands stating that the suit lands along with other properties belonged to Azmat Ali Kha Taluk, that the plaintiffs' predecessors Golam Gafur Sowdagar and Asgor Ali took settlement by registered deed dated 13th Magh, 1238 BS and that the settlement holders had tea plantations thereon. Thereafter they claimed "পরবর্তীক্রমে তদানিন্তন সরকার বাহাদুর উক্ত সম্পত্তির মধ্যে কতেক সম্পত্তি বাদীগনের পূর্ববর্তী গোলাম গফুর সওদাগর খাস দখলের প্রদান পূর্বক বাকী সম্পত্তি অতিরিক্ত সম্পত্তি হওয়ার কারনে তাহা সরকার বাহাদুর গ্রহন ক্রমে সরকারের আয় বৃদ্ধি কল্পে ১নং বিবাদীর দপ্তর পরিচালনার নিমিত্তে তাবৎ সম্পত্তির শাসন সংরক্ষনের ভার ১নং বিবাদীর উপর ন্যাস্ত করিলে.............................। 

 However, they have not changed the averments made in original paragraph No. 1 about their acquisition of title and allowed the same to remain in paragraph 1(ka). 

 8. Plaintiffs now claim that by way of settlement and successive transfers from the Azmot Ali Kha taluk they have acquired title in the suit lands. On the other hand, they claimed that the then Government handed over some lands in favour of Golam Gafur Sawdagor. If the suit lands were settled to Golam Gafur and Asgor Ali by registered deed, how the Government gave possession of some lands out of the said lands to Golam Gofur again is not clear to us? It is also not clear to us how the Government has taken over possession of the remaining lands and handed over possession of additional lands to Zila Parishad? The plea of taking over lands as excess is an absurd story in that, before the promulgation of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (SA & T Act) there was no law authorising the Government to take over possession of lands from any individual as excess lands other than by way of acquisition. All rent receiving interests of persons who have been described as rent receivers in clause (23) of section 3 of SA & Act, i.e., rent receiving interests of (i) proprietors (ii) tenure holders (iii) raiyats, (iv) under-raiyats (v) non-agricultural tenants in some cases, (vi) landlords in respect of service tenures (vii) lands in khas possession of rent receivers (viii) hat or bazar, (ix) fishery and (x) forest, etc. have been acquired on and from the date of publication of Gazette Notification dated 14th April, 1956. Admittedly, the suit lands had been recorded in the RS Khatian No. 981 in the name of the Zila Parishad and thus the lands vested in the defendant prior to 1950. Plaintiffs claim that the defendant petitioner has settled 0.58 acres of land out of 8.28 acres of land to Noor Hossain and, on the other hand, they have claimed proprietary right in the said lands, which claims are self contradictory. This inconsistency has cropped up after introducing the story of settlement by Exhibit 1 in order to avoid the plea of res judicata. 

 9. Mr TH Khan, learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiffs-opposite parties, fails to explain the' basis of the plaintiffs' title in the suit lands as pleaded in paragraphs 1 and 1(ka) of the plaint. The learned Advocate frankly concedes that there is some inconsistency in the pleadings about the acquisition of title in the suit lands but, according to the learned Advocate, this inconsistency will not stand in the way of plaintiffs getting decree in the suit since the RS Khatian No. 982 has been prepared in the name of plaintiff's predecessor. We find no force in the contention of the learned Advocate. 

 11. On a close look into the deed dated 13th Magh 1238 BS corresponding to 20th February 1877, with naked eyes, it will not be difficult to detect, even by a layman, over writings in various parts and use of separate inks and insertion of a few sentences with different inks at the bottom of the deed. The learned Advocate submits that as the document is very old one the words which were indistinct were overwritten for the purpose of understanding the recital in it. We failed to understand how a registered deed could have been made readable by overwriting by the party in whose favour it was filed? If there was existence of such registered deed, the plaintiffs could have obtained a certified copy thereof and filed the original along with the certified copy for the inspection of the Court. We have no hesitation to hold that this deed is a spurious document and that the Courts below have overlooked the over writings and interpolations in it. Besides that, there is no material on record to show that this deed attracts the suit lands. There is also no legal evidence to show that CS 130 kheyat khatian corresponds to RS plot No. 982 as claimed by the plaintiffs. The defendant has challenged this deed on the ground that the said deed does not attract the suit lands but the plaintiffs have not taken steps for relayment of the deed by way of local investigation. The trial Court answered the objection in the following manner: 

 12. How fallacious the observations of the trial Court are? We are shocked to notice these observations, which are apparently based upon inadmissible evidence. The plaintiffs have not examined this Shakhawat Hossain Chowdhury in the suit and he has not relayed the suit lands with Exhibit 1. Under such circumstances, how the alleged trace map prepared by said Shakhawat Hossain Chowdhury in connection with other purposes could be used as legal evidence in this suit and a decision was given holding that the said deed of 1877 attracted the CS khatian No. 130 and the RS khatian No. 982 as claimed by the plaintiffs? The plaintiffs instead of filing the original CS khatian, filed the certified copies as Exhibits 2 and 2(ka). These certified copies were obtained on 28th July, 2002 after institution of the suit just after amendment of the plaint. We find over writings in column 11 and therefore, it cannot be said to be an exaggeration if we hold that the plaintiffs cooked up a story by procuring the deed of 1877 and the CS khatian which do not relate to the suit lands after failing to establish their title in the earlier suit with a view to grab the suit lands. 

 13. The Courts below upon superficial consideration of these documents held, that the plaintiffs' had acquired title by adverse possession in the suit lands over 100 years by flouting the findings of this Court and the Appellate Division. This claim of acquisition of title on the basis of Exhibits 1 and 2 series is inconsistent with their claim made in paragraph 1(Ka) to the plaint. This inconsistency disproves the plaintiffs' acquisition of title in the suit lands. The Courts below overlooked these contradictory versions of the plaintiffs' claim in the suit lands and held that since the issues involved in the earlier suit were not identical with the issues involved in this suit, the suit was not barred by principle of res judicata. We hold that these findings of the Courts below are based upon misreading, non-consideration and superficial consideration of the evidence on record. 

 15. In the judgment (Exhibit B), this Court observed that the plaintiffs instituted the said suit in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong against the defendant-appellant (petitioner) praying for "declaration of their title and possession over the suit land." The petitioners by way of supplementary affidavit filed the plaint of Other Suit No. 95 of 1992 and the judgment of the trial Court. On perusal of the judgment, we find that the learned Joint District Judge has framed five issues and the issue No.5 reads as follows: "নালিশী সম্পত্তিতে বাদী পক্ষে স্বত্ত্ব দখল আছে কি নাঃ The learned Joint District Judge decreed the suit declaring "নালিশী সম্পত্তিতে বাদী পক্ষের স্বত্ত্ব স্বার্থ,  অধিকার ও দখল আছে মর্মে ঘোষিত হয়” The defendant- petitioner's resisted this suit on the plea of res judicata. The Courts below for reasons not known to us in order to avoid this plea not only misread the pleadings and the evidence on record, but also made inconsistent observations. The plaintiffs themselves admitted that they had instituted a suit earlier in respect of the suit lands and lost up to the Appellate Division. Therefore, there is no dispute that they were the plaintiffs in the earlier suit. The decree in FA No. 39 of 1995 (Exhibit B) clearly shows that the plaintiffs instituted the earlier suit. 

 16. Mr Khan submits that in the earlier suit the plaintiffs prayed for simple declaration without seeking title in the suit lands, and as the reliefs in both the suits are not distinct, this suit is not barred by res judicata. "There is no dispute that the defendant No.1 was the owner of the suit land and that the RS khatian No. 981 was accordingly, prepared in the name of the defendant No. 1. The plaintiffs-respondents claimed their title and possession over the suit land on the basis of the preparation of RS khatian in the name of Noor Hossain under superior landlord, the defendant No. 1 i.e. the District Council, in which he was in possession after taking settlement. Exhibit No.1 is the certified copy of the RS khatian of the suit land. It appears that this khadail was prepared in the name of the defendant No.1, the District Council, and under this khatian a sub-khatian being No. 982 was prepared in the name of Noor Hossain showing his possession in the remark column without describing his status either as raiyat or a sub-lessee though a jama of Taka 11 annas 8 and 3 pie are noted in this khatian in column meant for rent." The High Court Division observed in Exhibit B. "It is the definite case of the plaintiffs respondents that Noor Hossain was the owner in possession of the suit land in raiyati right under the defendant No. 1 i.e. the District Council. But the plaintiffs-respondents could not file any paper to show the alleged raiyati right of No or Hossain either on the basis of settlement or lease taken from the defendant No. 1 i.e. the District Council. Further, plaintiffs respondents could not file any rent receipt to show that Noor Hossain ever paid rent of the suit land to the defendant No. 1 i.e. the District Council or that the District Council ever realised any rent from Noor Hossain." 

 "True but the plaintiffs could not file any paper to show the alleged raiyati right of Nur Hossain on the basis of settlement or lease taken from defendant No.1. The High Court Division was well founded in law in holding that under the circumstances the plaintiffs have established a case of possession but not title. When they are in possession claiming raiyati settlement they cannot set up adverse possession either. They are not entitled to a declaration of title". 

 19. Mr TH Khan, learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-opposite parties, contends that a plea of res judicata is a mixed question of fact and law and a litigant, who is raising the said plea has to prove the said plea of adducing evidence. He argues that the defendant-petitioner has not filed the plaint and the judgment of the trial Court to show that the issues involved in the earlier suit and this suit are identical. Mr Khan contended that the findings of this Court in the earlier suit and the Appellate Division were erroneous since the suit lands were basically agricultural lands, after the SA&T Act came into force, the raiyats became maliks and therefore, the plaintiffs' possession in the suit lands had matured into title. It is further argued that since the earlier findings are based upon erroneous decision, the question of res judicata does not arise in this suit. In support of his contention Mr Khan has referred the case of Chairman, Chingleput Municipality vs M Murugesa Mudaliar and others, AlR 1933(Madras) 59. 

 "The principle of res judicata is based on the need of giving a finality to judicial decisions. What it says is that once a res judicata, it shall not be adjudged again. Primarily, it applies as between past litigation and future litigation. When a matter whether on a question of fact or a question of law has been decided between two parties in one suit or proceeding and the decision is final, either because no appeal was taken to a higher Court or because the appeal was dismissed, or no appeal lies, neither party will be allowed in a future suit or proceeding between the same parties to canvass the matter again. This principle of res judicata is embodied in relation to suits in section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure; but even where section 11 does not apply, the principle of res judicata has been applied by Courts for the purpose of achieving finality in litigation. The result of this is that the original Court as well as any higher Court must in any future litigation proceed on the basis that the previous decision was correct." 

 23. If the Court had no jurisdiction over a subject matter the decision of the Court is not res judicata in a subsequent suit. Mr Khan submits that since the issues involved in the earlier suit are not directly in issue in this suit, the decision in the earlier suit is not res judicata and, in support of his contention, he has referred the case of Durga Prasad Sharma vs Sadasib Biswal, AIR 1969 (Orissa),171. We do not dispute the proposition of law stated in that decision but in the earlier suit the plaintiffs claimed declaration of title and confirmation of possession and in this suit also they claimed similar reliefs besides other reliefs. The substantive relief in both the suits are for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in the suit lands. 

 25. Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been incorporated in the Code for the purpose of convenience of the parties that any issue which has been decided between the parties over the same subject matter cannot be reopened between the parties or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a Court competent to try such subsequent suit. If at the time of decision of the earlier suit the facts which have been raised in the subsequent suit were available to the plaintiffs, their remedy, in our view, lies by way of filing a review petition under Order XLVII, CPC but they cannot be allowed to file a fresh suit on the same subject matter with new facts. New pleas of different terms on the same facts cannot be entertained. 

 26. Even the subject matter of two suits may be different, the object of the suits, the reliefs and the causes of action may be different, but if the matter in issue in them is identical i.e. if the same title had been litigated before, res judicata will apply. A matter in issue between the parties is the right claimed by one party and denied by the other, and the claim of right from its very nature depends upon proof of facts and application of relevant law. The words "directly and substantially in issue" means if the matter was in issue directly in an earlier litigation and decided against a party then the decision would be res judicata in a subsequent proceeding. 

 "a petitioner is not entitled to make different pleas at different times so as to file more than one writ petition on the same facts. For a further plea the proper course would be to file a petition for review if such petition was maintainable. The general principle of res judicata is applicable in the writ petition also". 

 30. The principle of res judicata operates on the Court. It is the Court which is prohibited from trying the issue which was directly and substantially in issue in the earlier suit between the parties provided the Court trying the subsequent proceeding is satisfied that the earlier Court was competent to dispose of the suit and that the suit had been heard and finally decided by that Court. The principle of res judicata is based on the need of giving a finality to judicial decisions. The matter which prevents the same case being tried twice litigated is of general application and is not limited by the specific words of section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Res judicata applies also as between two stages in the same litigation to the extent that a Court, whether the trial Court or the higher Court having at an earlier stage decided a matter in one way will not allow the parties to reagitate the matter again at a subsequent stage of the same proceedings. The provisions of section 11 are mandatory and a litigant can avoid the provisions by taking advantage of section 44 of the Evidence Act, which defines with precision the grounds of such avoidance as fraud or collusion. The plaintiffs did not raise any plea of fraud or collusion in paragraph 5 of the plaint. They pleaded that while drawing up the plaint hurriedly, they failed to bring material facts and law in the plaint. This is not a legal ground for avoiding decisions given by proper Court having jurisdiction to try the suit. The plaintiff-opposite parties did not claim that the earlier Court had no jurisdiction to determine the issues involved in the suit as framed. The plaintiffs failed to establish their title by adverse possession in the suit lands in the earlier suit. 

 31. Even if it is assumed that the plaintiff hurriedly instituted the suit but after institution of the suit, they got sufficient time to amend the plaint. They did not amend the plaint and allowed it to dispose of finally. Even after institution of this suit on 1st February, 1999, they did not bring those facts of acquisition of title in the suit lands. They included those facts by way of amendment of the plaint on 11th May, 2002, after 3-1/2 years of the date of institution of the suit by bringing completely a new story. They did not amend the original claim made in paragraph 1 of the plaint, now in paragraph 1(ka), which averments are inconsistent with them. 

 32. Mr Khan submits that since both the Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiffs are in possession over 100 years relying upon the deed dated 20th February, 1877 Exhibit 1, this finding cannot be disturbed in exercise of revisional jurisdiction. It is unfortunate to note that the Courts below flagrantly flouted the findings of this Court and the Appellate Division and declared plaintiffs' title by adverse possession in the suit lands. We do not dispute that the concurrent findings of the Courts below are immune from interference by this Court in exercising revisional jurisdiction but if the concurrent findings are based upon misreading or non-consideration of the evidence or other materials on record or it has been founded on misconception or misapplication of law or on misinterpretation of a document or otherwise it is perverse, there is no legal bar to interfere with the concurrent findings. We find no substance in the contention of Mr Khan. Mr Khan finally submits that since there are concurrent findings, the matter should be remanded to the trial Court for enabling the plaintiffs an opportunity to relay Exhibit 1 by way of local investigation. As we observed that Exhibit 1 was a spurious document, we consider it unnecessary to remand the case for local investigation and so further prolong this ruinously protracted litigation because, in our view, the question of title in the suit lands was directly and substantially in issue between the plaintiffs and the defendant in the earlier suit and decided against the plaintiffs. 

 33. Since this Court and the Appellate Division clearly found that the plaintiffs failed to establish their title in the suit lands, we cannot sit over those judgments and decide whether or not those decisions were illegal or erroneous. The suit is apparently barred under section 11, CPC and therefore, the same is liable to be dismissed. The Courts below, on a misconception of law and fact, held that the suit was not barred by the principle of res judicata. The suit is not legally maintainable and the judgments of the Courts below are liable to be interfered with. We find merit in this Rule.

parties:
Gopal Chandra Das and others------ Plaintiff- Appellant-Petitioners 
Vs. 
Nikunja Behari Sukra Das and others ------ Defendant-Respondent- Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
Syed Abu Kowser Md. Dabirush-Shan, J. : This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 7-9-94 and 19-9-94 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Narayanganj, in Title Appeal No. 89 of 1986 affirming the judgment and decree dated 20-7-86 and 24-7-86 respectively passed by the Munsif, Bandar Upazila, Narayanganj, in Title Suit No. 38 of 1985 dismissing the suit should not be set aside. 

 2. The petitioners as plaintiff filed the Title Suit No. 34 of 1985 for declaration of title in the suit land stating, inter alia, that one Govinda Chandra Chakraborty was the superior landlord in Mirashi right in 'A' schedule land and while the same was under his management one Bhama Baishnabi was given shelter in the suit land by the said Govinda and CS record was recorded in the name of the said Bhama Baishnabi. About 60 years ago the said Bhama Baishnabi died leaving one heir and thereafter said Govinda, superior landlord of the Estate, took the 'A' schedule land in his khas possession. In the "B" schedule land said Govinda Chandra was owner in possession as Mirashi right, Govinda died leaving only two sons namely, Mukunda and Gopal. By an amicable settlement between these two brothers Mukunda got the suit land. Mukunda in exercising his sixteen annas right, title and interest in the suit properties approached to plaintifs father for taking settlement of the suit properties on payment of reasonable rent for the suit land and thereafter Mukunda gave rioyti settlement by executing an unregistered Hukum Nama with respect to the suit properties in the Bengali year 1343 BS on 17th Poush corresponding to 1936 in favour of Krishna Mohan Das, the father of the plaintiffs. Krishna Mohan Das was owner in possession of the suit properties by getting settlement and he died in the year 1956 at his own house in the suit Mouza leaving behind three sons, the plaintiffs who by inheritance became the owner and possessed the entire suit land for more than 12 years uninterruptedly and have been paying rent to the Government and that on 17-8-85 for the first time they came to know from the local Tahsilder that the suit properties have been treated as vested properties by the defendants No. 5 and 6 as the properties were earlier recorded in favour of defendant Nos. 1-4 and also Tahsilder refused to accept the rent from the plaintiffs. The defendants have no right, title and possession in the suit properties and SA Khatian has been wrongly prepared in faovur of the defendant Nos. 1-4 due to such recording in favour of the defendant No. 1-4 a cloud of doubt in the right, title and interest of the plaintiff in the suit land and to dispel such cloud and doubt plaintiffs have constrained to file the suit. 

 3. The defendant No. 5 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegation and contending, inter alia, that the owners of the suit properties Mukunda and Gopal Chakraborty are the sons of Govinda Chandra who are the citizens of India and they have been living in India permanently having citizenship for which the suit property have been enlisted as Vested Property. One Abdul Barek prayed for lease of the suit properties and an investigation to the effect is going on and that Gopal Chandra, Santi Chandra Das and Abdul Matin are the legal possessors in the suit properties which have already been enlisted as vested property and that the plaintiffs' right, title and interest or possession in the suit property has been enlisted as vested property, as such, the plaintiffs cannot get any relief in this suit. Hence, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 4. During the trial plaintiff examined 2 witnesses and the defendant examined only 1 witness Tahsilder to prove their respective cases. The learned trial Court after hearing both the parties and perusing the evidence on record document and exhibits and also the Hokum Nama came to a finding that the plaintiff failed to establish his title in the suit land by producing any document i.e. title deed. On the other hand, the defendant examined Tahsilder Md Safiuddin who stated in his evidence that the original owner of the land Mukunda, son of Govinda migrated to India and has been living in India permanently, as such, the suit property has been enlisted as vested property in the census report and the plaintiff has been illegally possessing the suit land. The learned trial Court after hearing dismissed the suit of the plaintiff by his judgment and decree dated 20-7-76 and 24-7-86 respectively. 

 5. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree dated 20-7-86 and 24-7-86 passed by the learned Munsif, Bandar Upazila, Narayanganj, the plaintiff preferred an appeal being Title Appeal No. 89 of 1986 before the learned District Judge, Narayanganj and the appeal was ultimately heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Narayanganj who after hearing was pleased to dismiss the appeal by his judgment and decree dated 7-9-94 and 19-9- 94 respectively. 

 7. Mr Faruque Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant- petitioner submits that the lower appellate Court and also the trial Court without applying their judicial mind and without proper assessment of the evidence on record and also the legal point involved in this case came to a wrong and erroneous finding in dis- missing the suit of the plaintiff. Next, the learned Counsel submits that the plaintiff since 1343 BS corresponding to 1936 AD has been living in the suit land by erecting the houses after obtaining the Hokum Nama from the original owner Mukunda and, as such, the plaintiff have acquired a good title by way of right of adverse possession. The defendant also admitted and gave a suggestion in cross- examination to the plaintiff that he has been illegally possessing the suit land. Both the lower appellate Court as well as the trial Court also observed in their judgment that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit property illegally by way of private dhakila and Hokum Nama which has got no leg to stand in the eye of law and in this connection both the courts relied upon a decision reported in 30 DLR (SC) 41 wherein it has been clearly stated that the private document cannot be taken into notice and consideration and marked as exhibit without any formal proof unless the requirement of such proof is waived by the opposite party. This observation made by the courts below are not applicable and legally tenable in the context of the present suit. The learned Counsel further submits that both the courts below failed to appreciate the legal aspect of the case with regard to section 28 of the Limitation Act which reads as follows: 

 Section 28 Acquisition of title by adverse possession- 

 "Though the transfer by invalid document does not confer title, the transferee when continues in possession of the immovable property for more than the statutory period of 12 years uninterrupted on the basis therefof he acquired title to the said property by adverse possession notwithstanding the defect in the documents. 

 Thus when there is an invalid transfer in favour of a person and he holds possession of the property transferred as transferee, his possession is in his own right and adverse to the transferee. If he continues in possession of immoveable property for more than twelve years he will acquire an indefeasible title." 

 8. The learned Counsel submits that the plain- tiff has been possessing and living in the suit land since 1936 and the case was filed on 20-11-85 i.e. after the lapse of 49 years. Enemy Property Ordinance was promulgated in the year 1965 long after the execution of Hokum Nama by the original owner Mukunda and since then plaintiff has been living in the suit property. If, according to section 28 of the Limitation Act, the period is computed from the year 1936, then the statutory period of 12 years would expire on 1948 to extinguish the right of possession even by the original owner Mukunda. The Enemy Property Ordinance, subsequently a vested property when it was promulgated, did not give any retrospective effect, as such, the plaintiff acquired title by adverse possession after the expiry of 12 year. The learned Counsel finally submits that the lower appellate Court failed to apply his judicial mind in considering the most important legal aspect of the case occasioning failure of justice which is liable to be interfered by this Court. 

 10. On a meticulous examination of the evidence on record, exhibits, dakhilas, Hokum Nama and other connected papers and the judgment of both the Courts below it transpires that the lower appellate Court as well as the trial Court committed error in law as well as on facts. Both the courts below in their judgment observed that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land illegally and defendant also admitting that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land since long but plaintiff is possessing the suit land illegally. But prior to the institution of the title suit by the plaintiff the peaceful possession of the plaintiff was never disturbed by anybody and no notice was served by the vested property authority upon the plaintiff to the effect that the suit property has been enlisted as vested property. The Vested Property Authority could not prove any notice or paper to show that the notice was served upon the plaintiff by the Authority through DW Tahsilder. The vested property authority failed to prove any legal foundation to enlist the property in the vested property list. In this connection I like to rely on the decision in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Paresh Chandra Gharami reported in 50 DLR (AD) 70 wherein it has been stated. 

 13. The discussion made above and the facts and legal position of the case the impugned judgment and decree dated 7-9-94 and 19-9-94 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Narayanganj, in Title Appeal No. 89 of 1986 affirming the judgment and decree dated 20-7- 86 and 24-7-86 respectively passed by the Munsif, Bandar Upazila, Narayanganj, in Title Suit No. 38 of 1985 is hereby set aside and the Title Suit No. 89 of 1986 filed by the plaintiff is hereby decreed.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1138 of 2006.
parties:
Kulsuma Khatun ------ Petitioner
vs
Rahman Sobhan ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
2. The short fact leading to the filing of the leave petition is that the suit land is originally recorded as Government khas land during the time of CS operation. The suit land was sold in auction for arrear of rent in Certificate Case No. 25/20-21 on 11-9-1922 and auction-purchased by one Abala Sundari in the benami of Upendra Lal Chowdhury and Prafulla Bala Debi and got delivery of possession through Court. Upendra Lal Chowdhury by registered deed dated 22-9-1922 relinquished his claim in favour of Abala Sundari and Abala Sundari got delivery of possession on 31-5-1923. Prafulla Bala by registered kabala dated 22-9-1930 sold her share of land to Abala Sundari and delivered possession to her. RS Khatian finally stands recorded in the name of Abala Sundari. The suit land was hillock and full of jungle. Abala Sundari converted the same by expending huge amount of money. Abala Sundari while in possession made an agreement for sale with the predecessor of the plaintiffs with a consideration money of Taka 2500 and she took Taka 2000 as advance and delivered possession to plaintiffs' predecessor on 26th of Kartik, 1340 BS. After purchase the predecessor of the plaintiffs constructed kutcha and pucca houses upon the schedule land and he was in peaceful possession. After the death of their predecessor the plaintiffs are in possession upon the suit schedule land and they acquired title over the same under section 54 (A) of the Transfer of Property Act. The defendant Nos. 2 to 14 have got no right, title, interest and possession over the suit land but they have fraudulently managed to have their names recorded in the BS khatian and now they are claiming title over the suit land. Hence the plaintiffs filed the present suit for declaration of their title. 

 4. The learned Assistant Judge by order No. 46 dated 15-10-1992 dismissed the said Miscellaneous case. As against this order, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 310 of 1992 and by judgment and decree dated 23-8-1998, the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong allowed the appeal on setting aside the judgment and order dated 15-10-1992 and restored Title Suit No. 183 of 1990 to its original file and number. Thereafter the plaintiff-petitioners, filed a review petition before the same Court to reconsider and set aside the judgment and order passed on 23-8-1998, which was ultimately rejected on 22-11-1998. Thereafter the plaintiff-petitioners having been aggrieved by the judgment and order dated 23-11-1998 preferred Civil Revision No. 4334 of 1998 in the High Court Division. After hearing the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division discharged the Rule. Thereafter being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division the plaintiff-petitioners filed this civil petition for leave to appeal. 

 5. Mr Md Nawab Ali, the learned Advocate-on-Record for the petitioners, submits that the case of the defendant-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 before the trial Court was that the summons was not duly served on them and that they were not aware of the institution of the suit but they did not claim in their petition that their addresses given in the cause-title of the suit was wrong but in spite of this position the learned Subordinate Judge as well as the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in making out a third case. He lastly, submits that the Single Bench of the High Court Division committed an error of law affirming the judgment and order of the appellate Court below without any legal and valid reasonings. Therefore the judgment of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside for the ends of justice.
