caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1469 of 2004
parties:
Amalendu Kar @ Nepal and another ------ Petitioners
VS
Abdul Halim Bhuiyan being dead his heirs and heiresses: Md. Moazzem Hossain and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Amin J: This petition for leave to appeal has been filed against the judgment passed on March 1, 2004 by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1600 of 1990 discharging the Rule obtained against the judgment and decree dated May, 30 1990 of the Court of Additional District judge, Kishoreganj in Other Class Appeal No. 35 of 1989 reversing the judgment and decree dated December 24, 1988 of the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Kishoreganj in Title Suit No. 621 of 1984 declaring the right, title and interest of the plaintiff in the land in suit and further declaring that the decree dated April 16, 1979 passed in Other Class Suit No. 46 of 1976 of the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Mymensingh is illegal and not binding on the plaintiffs and for restoration of possession of the land in suit to the plaintiffs. 

 3. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 by filing written statements stating, inter alia, that the land in suit belonged to Narmada Kumari Ghose and she never settled the land with the plaintiffs predecessor, that the hukumnama and the rent receipt filed by the plaintiffs are forged and fabricated, that plaintiffs did not acquire any right, title and interest in the land in suit and the decree obtained in Other Class Suit No. 34 of 1983 was fraudulent since the persons who were in possession of the land in suit were not impleaded in the said suit, that the defendants and their predecessor got possession of the land in suit through Court, that in Other Class Suit No. 34 of 1983 plaintiffs did not pray for recovery of possession and the defendant No.1 was not impleaded in the said suit, that the said suit Was filed seeking mere declaration of title and the decree therein was obtained by practicing fraud, that land in suit was not wrongly recorded in the name of the Government and the plaintiffs being unauthorised persons notice was served for eviction, that plaintiffs handed over possession of the land in suit on June 26, 1966 and since then plaintiffs have no right, title and possession in the land in suit, that Government taking possession of the land in suit let out one room to the defendant No.2 and defendant No.1 on the basis of the bainapatra took possession of the remaining portion of the building in 1972. In 1978 the contesting defendant vacated the room and since then office of BNP was there and using the room as its organizing office, that defendant No.1 filed Other Class Suit No.46 of 1976 against Narmada Kumari Ghose seeking specific performance of contract for sale of land and for recovery of possession, that the suit was contested by the Government by filing written statement, that the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, that defendant No.1 obtained kabala through Court and got possession upon evicting the unauthorised occupiers including the organizing office of BNP, that defendant No.1 transferred .14 acre of land along with the building from the southern portion of the land in suit to defendant No.3 and therein defendant No.3 running a restaurant, that defendant No.1 handed over remaining portion of the building to defendant No.2, that defendant Nos.2 and 3 are in possession of the land in suit, that defendant No.1 has gifted one decimal of land from plot No. 10161 to defendant Nos. 4 and 5 and they are in possession. 

 4. The trial Court on the finding that the defendant No.1 on the basis of the decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 46 of 1976 did not acquire any right, title and interest in the land in suit, that transfers by the defendant No.1 to defendant Nos.2 and 3 and others were illegal and that by the said transfers defendant Nos.2 and 3 have not acquired any right, title and interest in the land in suit, that plaintiffs were in possession of the land in suit till the date of their dispossession on January 30, 1984 and as such plaintiffs are entitled to get back the possession. 

 5. It was also held by the trial Court that the decree in Other Class Suit No. 46 of 1976 having not been challenged by the Government and that the said decree having been maintained by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and that the plaintiffs' 'hukumnama' and the 'dakhila' appears to be not genuine but they are in possession of the land in suit is evident from the fact the Government served notice directing the plaintiffs to surrender possession and thus plaintiffs by their possession for long period have acquired title by adverse possession. 

 6. The contesting defendant went on appeal. The appellate Court allowed the appeal on the finding that plaintiffs have not prayed for any decree as to acquiring title by adverse possession and that decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 46 of 1976 as was maintained up to the Appellate Division the plaintiffs acquired no title in the land in suit. The plaintiffs moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained Rule. 

 7. The High Court Division on consideration of the materials on record held that because of the decree in Other Class Suit No. 46 of 1976 which was maintained up to the Appellate Division and in execution thereof plaintiff of that suit having had obtained the kabala, the plaintiffs of the instant suit have not acquired any title in the land in suit and they have also on possession in the land in suit, that plaintiffs obtained decree in Other Class Suit No. 34 of 1983 at a time subsequent to the obtaining of possession of the land in suit by the defendant No.1 in execution of the land in suit by the defendant No.1 in execution of the decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 46 of 1976. The High Court Division affirmed the finding of the lower appellate Court as to non-acquiring of title by the plaintiffs on the basis of their alleged settlement. The High Court Division also affirmed the finding of the lower appellate Court that the plaintiff did not acquire any title by adverse possession since they had no case like that in their pleading. 

 8. We have heard the learned Advocate and perused the materials on record. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted that High Court Division was in error in not setting aside the judgment of the lower appellate Court reversing the judgment of the trial Court decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiffs on the finding that the plaintiffs have acquired right, title and interest in the land in suit by adverse possession. The contention of the learned Advocate is of no merit since from the materials on record it is seen that they claimed title on the basis of settlement from the original owner but that case was not established before the trial Court and in that context the plaintiffs prayed for a decree as regard their title on the basis of their alleged adverse possession and the trial Court without adverting to the materials on record particularly decree in Other Class Suit No. 46 of 1976 on the basis whereof defendant No.1 had acquired title and also got possession of the land decreed the suit. When the attention of the learned Advocate was drawn to the finding of the High Court Division as well as the lower appellate Court, that plaintiffs did not plead any case of acquiring title in the land in suit by adverse possession and consequent thereupon the decree passed by the trial Court was not sustainable in law, he felt difficulty to support the decree passed by the trial Court in favour of the plaintiffs.
case_type_name: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal

parties:
Joynab Begum and others ----- Appellants
Vs
Shaheb Ali Akunji & others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam J: This appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 9-8- 2000 of the High Court. Division passed in Civil Revision No. 3175 of 1993 making absolute the Rule obtained against the judgment and decree dated 21-8-1993 of the learned Additional District Judge, Bagerhat passed in Title Appeal No. 207 of 1989 affirming those of dated 28-7-1987 of the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Bagerhat passed in Title Suit No. 94 of 1982 decreeing the suit. 

 2. Late Kawsar Ali Shaikh, the predecessor in interest of the appellants, filed the above Title Suit No. 94 of 1982 for specific performance of contract on the averments that late Noor Ali Akunji, the defendant No.1 in the above suit and the predecessors in interest of the respondent Nos. 5 to 12, was the owner in possession of the suit land measuring 3.93 acres and he on 29-11-1976 entered into an agreement with the plaintiff for sale of the suit land at a consideration of Taka 30,000 and on receipt of Taka 25,000 as advance he made over the possession of the suit land to the plaintiff and in the said agreement it was stipulated that the, defendant No.1 shall get back the possession of suit land in case of his refund of the advance amount of Taka 25,000 within the month of Chaitra 1386 BS and in default, the defendant No. 1 shall execute and register sale deed within the month of Baisakh 1387 BS in favour of the plaintiff on receipt of balance amount Taka 5,000; the defendant No. 1 having failed to refund Taka 25,000 within Chaitra 1386 BS, the plaintiff on tendering the balance consideration money requested the defendant No. 1 several times to execute and register the sale deed but the defendant No. 1 deferred the same on this or that plea and on 30-4-1982, corresponding to 16 Baisakh 1389 BS, he finally refused to execute and register the sale deed. 

 8. As it appears the High Court Division just stating the submissions of the learned Advocate and referring to 42 DLR 86 and 1972 PLD (SC) 27 held that since DW 1 deposed that she did not know about the contract for sale and the defendants were bonafide purchasers for value without notice the onus shifted to the plaintiff to prove that the defendants had the knowledge of contract and the plaintiff having failed to discharge the onus is not entitled to obtain decree for specific performance of contract. 

 (b) any other person claiming under him by a title arising subsequently to the contract, except a transferee for value who had paid his money in good faith and without notice of the original contract. 

 10.It will thus be noticed that under the above provision of law, a contract can be specifically performed against any other person claiming title to the property arising subsequently to the original contract but an exception has been made in the case of transferee for value who has paid money to the transferor in good faith and without notice of the original contract. It is, therefore, for the transferee to prove that he was a transferee in good faith and without notice of the original contract for valuable consideration. 

 "In their Lordships opinion, the section lays down a general rule that the original contract may be specifically enforced against a subsequent transferee, but allows an exception to that general rule, not to the transferor, but to the transferee, and, in their Lordships opinion, it is clearly for the transferee to establish the circumstances which, will allow him to retain the benefit of transfer which prima facie he had no right to get. Further, the subsequent transferee is the person within whose knowledge the facts as to whether he has paid and whether he had notice of the original contract lie, and the provisions of section 103 and 106, Evidence Act, 1872, have a bearing on the question." 

 14. It is thus quite clear that in a suit for specific performance of contract the onus lies heavily on the person whose title arises subsequent to the contract to sell and he must prove that he is a transferee for value and has paid the money in good faith and without notice of the original contract.

parties:
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Comilla and others ------ Appellants.
VS
Md. Abdur Rob and others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
2. The respondents, as plaintiffs, filed Title Suit No. 89 of 1995 in the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), First Court, Comilla, seeking declaration of title and, after hearing, the above suit was dismissed. Being aggrieved the plaintiffs preferred First Appeal No. 79 of 1990 before the High Court Division and filed therein an application under Order 6 Rule 17 CPC praying for Adding the prayer for recovery of khas possession in the plaint on payment of advalorem court fees contending that unless the above consequential relief of recovery of possession, in respect of the two portions of the suit property in respect of which the plaintiffs claimed khas possession through their monthly tenants, are added in the plaint the plaintiffs will suffer irreparable loss and injury. The defendant-appellants by filing counter affidavit opposed the above prayer. The High Court Division, after hearing, allowed the above prayer and sent back the suit to the trial court for fresh trial with the direction that the suit should be disposed of after giving adequate opportunities to the parties. 

 6. As it appears the High Court Division passed the impugned judgment and order holding that the original suit is for declaration of title simplicitor and the proposed amendment is sought for recovery of khas possession in respect to some portions of the suit land in which the defendants denied the title and possession of the plaintiffs in those portions and unless the proposed amendment is allowed the plaintiff will suffer irreparable loss and injury and the whole purpose of the suit will be frustrated and that the proposed amendment will not in any way change the nature and character of the suit.

parties:
Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka & others ------ Appellants
Versus
Shamirunnessa Bibi, being dead her heirs:-1(a) Hasan Ali Matbar & others ------Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Short facts are that the respondents' predecessor filed Title Suit No.208 of 1984 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Dhaka for declaration of title in the land described in the schedule of the plaint and for further declaration that the Memo No.560 dated 09.06.1984 issued by the defendant No.6 (Sub Divisional Engineer, P.W.D., Sub-Division No.1 Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka) is illegal, unlawful, without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiff. 

 3. The defendants entered appearance in the said suit and prayed for time to file written statement but ultimately no written statement having been filed the suit was fixed for ex parte hearing on 06.11.1984. On that date the defendants prayed for time to file written statement but no written statement was filed and the suit was fixed on 28.11.1984 for ex parte hearing. The date so fixed for ex parte hearing was shifted to 12.12.1984 by the Court and on that date the suit was heard ex parte and decreed. Thereafter the defendants filed an application under Order 9 Rule 13 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and thereupon the aforementioned Miscellaneous Case was stated. The prayer for restoration of the original suit to its file and number was opposed by the plaintiff. The trial court dismissed the case holding that the petitioners of the miscellaneous case failed to make out a case for setting aside the ex parte decree. Thereupon the defendants took an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No.45 of 1993 before the District Judge, Dhaka. The appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka and the same was alloyed and the ex parte decree dated a 12/12.1984 was set aside and the original shit was restored to file and number. The plaintiff then moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained Rule. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute upon observing that the appellate court was in error in not holding that the defendants were guilty of latches in conducting their case and thereupon caused failure of justice in allowing the miscellaneous appeal. As against the order dated 20.04.2002 of the High Court Division making the Rule absolute the appellants filed an application under Order 47 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil procedure seeking review of the aforesaid judgment and order and the High Court Division by the order dated 20.05.2002 rejected the review application summarily upon observing that no case for review was made out. 

 4. Leave was granted to consider the submission that the entire suit plot No.533 was acquired by the Government and the respondent No.1 obtained the ex parte decree by making false statement on the basis of forged document and as such the impugned judgments and orders dated 20.04.2002 and 20.05.2002 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1578 of 1993 are liable to be set aside for ends of justice and further submission that the respondent No.1 previously filed a suit being Title Suit No.222 of 1979 against the present appellants for the same relief and the same was dismissed for default and the respondent No.1 having not filed any Miscellaneous Case or appeal against the said order dated 05.03.1975 the present suit has been filed suppressing the said facts in could ex parte decree was also obtained and as such the impugned judgment and order dated 20.04.2002 and 20.05.2002 passed in Civil Revision No.1578 of 1993 are liable to be set aside. 

 8. The learned Attorney General submits that after final publication of gazette notification dated 20.02.1950 the right, title and interest if any, of the original owner in the acquired land including the suit plot had already extinguished and once the property was acquired and gazette notification published, the same vested in the government and cannot be released in the manner as claimed by plaintiff. In support of his argument the learned Attorney General cited the case of Director of Housing & Settlement Vs. Abdul Majid Howlader and others reported in 9 MLR (AD) 73 and submitted that in that case it was held that the settled law is that upon acquisition of particular property the same vests in the Government and that being the position in law the prayer for release made by the Respondents was totally misconceived one since under the law they were not entitled to have the property released. Accordingly suit so filed seeking release of the property was not legally well advised one as well as was not entertainable in law. He further submitted that in the instant case the validity of acquisition of the property in question has not been disputed. He next submitted that the undisputed position is that the property in suit was acquired under the provision of (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 and to that respect gazette notification has been published making the acquisition final and vesting the property in suit in the Government. As per provision of law on the publication of the gazette notification the property acquired vests in the Government and consequent thereupon Government becomes the owner of the property. The person whose property is acquired under the Act and consequent thereupon vests in the Government, is not entitled to claim any interest in the land so acquired. In that view of the matter there was no scope for the plaintiffs, who have no interest of any kind in the land in suit, to seek for a declaration that they are entitled to get the property released. 

 12. From the plaint of Title Suit No.208 of 1984 of the 1st  Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka brought by Mrs. Shamirunnessa Bibi wife of Hasan Ali against Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and others it appears that the plaintiff sought declaration of her title over the entire 2.30 acres of land of C .S. Plot No.533 of C. S. Khatian No.112 of Mouza Tejkunipara, P.S. Tejgaon, Dhaka although according to plaintiffs own case 30 decimals of land was under acquisition, 

 14. The learned Attorney General in this connection submitted that to avoid the embargo of section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948, the plaintiff brought the suit claiming the entire 2.30 acres of land of Suit Plot No.533. The plaintiff also sought correction of record of right in respect of entire 2.30 acres of land although she claims 100 acres of land only and not the entire 2.30 acres. The learned Attorney General further submitted that although the plaintiff cleverly sought declaration of title over the entire 2.00 acres of land of the suit plot but that will not bring the suit out of the mischief of section 14A of the Act. 

 16. We have already noticed that in this case ex-parte decree was passed on 12.12.1984 in Title Suit No.208 of 1993 and in Miscellaneous Appeal No.45 of 1993 the Ex-parte decree was set aside and the original suit was restored to file and number. The High Court Division making the Rule absolute in the revisional application restored the ex-parte decree to its original position. Therefore, the fact remains that there was no contested hearing of the suit and the defendants could not place their case and other materials before the court for proper adjudication. 

 19. Since there are some patent incongruities in the plaint of Title Suit No.208 of 1994 brought by the plaintiff Samirunnessa Bibi as noticed earlier the ex parte decree dated 12.12.1984 ex-facie is not sustainable.

parties:
Ibn Sina Trust ------ Petitioner 
Vs 
Arab Bangladesh Bank Ltd and anr ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md Arayesuddin J: This Rule was issued calling upon opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 1-4-2004 by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 105 of 2004 rejecting an application under Order XXI, rule 29 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for staying all further proceedings of Money Execution Case No. 89 of 2003 pending before the Artha Rin Adalat, Court, No. 3 Dhaka regarding auction sale of the petitioner's property till disposal of Title Suit No. 105 of 2004 should not be set aside. 

 2. Relevant fact to dispose of the Rule, in brief, is that the petitioner is a Charitable Organisation registered under the Societies Act, 1982 having good reputation and countrywide name and fame. The petitioner organisation claims to be the lawful owner of the suit property. They did not take any loan from the opposite party Bank. They are not also a guarantor for the money borrowed from the Bank. Yet the opposite party Bank obtained a decree for realisation of the loan money, availed and enjoyed by the opposite party No. 2. In the impugned suit petitioner was imploaded as defendant No. 4. The summons and notice were suppressed and playing fraud upon the Court as well as the parties plaintiff-opposite party No.1 obtained the impugned judgment and decree. Petitioner had no relief under Order XXI, rule 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure as they are not third party. No relief can also be claimed by filing Miscellaneous Case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code since the suit has been dismissed ex-parte against the petitioner. Therefore, the petitioner was compelled to file a separate suit being Title Suit No. 105 of 2004 in the Court of the Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka challenging the fraudulent decree in view of the decision passed in CPLA No. 572 of 1994 reported in 1995 BLD (AD) 35. In this suit petitioner filed a petition under Order XXI, rule 29 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for stay of all further proceeding of the Artha Jari Case No. 89 of 2003 pending before the Artha Rin Adalat, Court No. 3. Dhaka regarding the auction sale of the petitioner's property till disposal of Title Suit No. 105 of 2004 which was rejected by the Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka on 1-4-2004 in Title Suit No. 105 of 2004. Being aggrieved, petitioner moved this Court in revisional Jurisdiction and obtained the Rule. 

 4. On behalf of the plaintiff-petitioner, the learned Advocate Mr Enayet Hossain Khan submitted the petitioner is a reputed welfare trust extending medical help to the general public throughout the country and they had no need of money to solicit any loan from the Bank. The petitioner purchased the suit land in 1986. At the time of purchase their vendor did not supply the original deed on the plea that it was lost. The petitioner believed the vendor. Petitioner is in possession of the suit land. But subsequently, their vendor, by suppressing the fact of the alleged transfer took loan from the bank by mortgaging the suit property on deposit of the 'title deed. The Bank, without making any further enquiry about the title and possession, allowed the loan by keeping the original deed. The vendor became a defaulter. As a result Bank filed Title Suit No. 116 of 1998 for realisation of the loan money. In the suit petitioner was made defendant No. 4. But the Bank in collusion with the borrower suppressed all the summons and notices and obtained ex-parte decree against this petitioner. But contested decree was passed against the borrower. The Bank put the decree in execution by filing Money Execution Case No. 89 of 2003. In the judgment the trial Court observed that the borrower has no title in the other lands. So, the land possessed by the petitioner measuring 17 decimals has been put to auction. At the time the petitioner came to know of the impugned judgment and decree. In the meantime the perfod of limitation for filing Miscellaneous Case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was over. He submitted that finding no other alternative petitioner instituted a separate suit as per decision of the Appellate Division and filed a petition under Order XXI, rule 29 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for staying the further proceeding of the Money Execution Case No. 89 of 2003. The learned trial Court without considering the petition on merit rejected the same which is not tenable in law. He has further submitted that the trial Court ought to have passed the order of stay till disposal of the suit. To strengthen his argument the learned Advocate submitted that if the suit of the petitioner is decreed and in the meantime he is dispossessed from the suit land there would be further litigation and the very purpose of the suit will be frustrated. The learned Advocate submitted that honorable Appellate Division has categorically opined that the allegation of non-service of summons in a suit of Artha Rin Adalat can be challenged by filing separate suit. 

 6. We have perused the petition, the Rule and the counter-affidavit and heard the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides. It is admitted that the petitioner was defendant No. 4 in Title Suit No. 116 of 1998. Petitioner's contention is that he did not receive any summons and notices of that suit. So he could not contest. His further allegation is that plaintiff and defendant Nos. 1 and 2 collusively suppressed the summons by practicing fraud upon the court. We have perused the judgment of our honorable Appellate Division delivered in CPLA No. 572 of 1994 in the case of Md Mozammel Hoque vs Sonali Bank and another. In that judgment the Appellate Division has given the exhaustive guideline in para 3 which runs as follows: 

 With this exhaustive findings their Lordships of the Appellate Division was pleased to dismiss the petition for leave to appeal. In the above findings a clear guideline has been given. A separate suit is not barred provided his remedies under the Artha Rin Adalat Act stood barred at the time of filing of the suit for no fault of his own. Annexure A is the judgment of Title Suit No. 116 of 1998. The suit has been decreed in preliminary form against defendant Nos. 1-2 and 3 and dismissed ex-parte against defendant Nos. 3-4. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that he cannot claim any relief before the Artha Rin Adalat. We are unable to accept this submission in view of the application of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Artha Rin Adalat, Act, 1990 under which the suit Was filed. Section 5(4) of the Act is clear to the effect. Therefore, we find that the door of the Code of Civil Procedure is still' open to the petitioner if he can prove that no summons of notices were served upon him and he had no knowledge of the suit. The learned Advocate submitted that petitioner has no scope to file Miscellaneous Case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure as the suit has been dismissed ex parte against him. The definition of decree has been misconceived. The leaned Advocate for opposite party No. 1 also admits that petitioner can seek his relief under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure if he can over come limitation.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree (FA) No. 76 of 1998.
parties:
Rafia Begum   ------ Plaintiff-Appellant
vs
Afroza Bewa and others   ------ Defendants- Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The appellant as plaintiff filed the above suit against original defendant Dr GM Enamul Huq (now dead) for simple declaration of her title in the suit land described in the schedule of the plaint alleging, inter alia, that she was married with the original defendant on 29-11-1984 on fixation of dower of Taka 60,001 out of which Taka 16,000 was shown paid in the Kabinnama. While they were living as husband and wife on 28-1-1985 the original defendant divorced her and on 12-2-1985 fraudulently created a Kabinnama showing her marriage with him for the second time and less amount of dower. They continued to live together as husband and wife as before and she gave birth to a son on 5-5-1986. The defendant constructed a building in the suit land by her money and began to live there with her. On 25-11-1989 the defendant in his rented house at Nisindara orally gifted her the suit property in presence of her father in lieu of balance dower and money given by her for construction of the building and also delivered possession of the same to her. Since then she had been living there on payment of municipal taxes, rent, etc. through her defendant husband who had no subsisting interest therein. Later on when her relationship with the defendant became strained over his claim of dowry the defendant through his sister's son Rabu asked the appellant to quit and vacate the building. Hence she filed the suit. 

 3. The original defendant contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the defendant was a qualified medical practitioner; that the appellant was his second wife; that the defendant by his own money amounting Taka 5 lac constructed the building on the suit land and had been living there with the appellant; that he never gifted the suit property to the appellant; that he divorced the appellant on account of her misbehavior and that the appellant had no right, title and interest in the suit property. 

 5. At the trial in order to prove the plaint case, the appellant alone deposed as PW 1. No document was admitted into evidence on her side. On the other hand, 3 DWs were examined and some rent receipts, a municipal tax receipt, an electricity bill, etc. were admitted into evidence on the side of the defendants. The learned Subordinate Judge, on consideration of the evidence on record, dismissed the suit with the finding that the plaintiff-appellant failed to prove the alleged oral gift and her title in the suit property on basis of the same. 

 8. Mr Amanullah the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents, has made submission opposing the appeal and supporting the impugned judgment and decree. He has submitted that the appellant failed to avail the opportunity given to her for adducing further evidence in proving the alleged oral gift and, as such, there is no ground of sending the suit on remand for retrial setting aside the impugned judgment and decree. According to him, the suit has been rightly dismissed due to the failure of the appellant to prove her title in the suit land and there is no reason of interfering with the impugned judgment and decree, 

 9. Undisputedly, the appellant was the second wife of the deceased original defendant, the owner of the suit land, It is also an admitted fact that the deceased defendant constructed a building on the suit land and used to live there with the appellant, It is also not disputed that the defendant divorced the appellant on 12-11-1991. Eleven days after such divorce on 23-11-1991 the appellant filed this suit asserting that the defendant on 25-11-1989 in his rented house in presence of her father orally gifted her the suit property. The deceased original defendant in his written statement denied alleged gift, In that context now the question is, whether the original defendant orally gifted the suit property to the appellant and she acquired right, title and interest therein on that basis, 

 10. The appellant as PW 1 deposed supporting the plaint case. No one was examined to corroborate her and not a single scrap of paper was admitted into evidence on her side, She stated that the defendant in lieu of unpaid dower orally gifted the suit property to her on 25-11-1989 in presence of her father in his rented house at Nisindara Housing Estate and thereafter delivered. possession to her, She did not give the date of delivery of possession and her going into possession, Her father in whose presence the defendant allegedly gifted the suit property had not been examined without explanation. She did not disclose to anybody the factum of alleged oral gift, She gave no evidence as to her acceptance of such gift, She did not get her name mutated in the revenue office or in the municipality and never paid rent, municipal tax or electric bills. Exhibits B series, C and D show that the rent, municipal tax and the electric bills were paid by the deceased defendant himself even after the alleged gift. Thus she did not exercise her ownership in the suit property, D WI, the respondent No, 1 (kha) and one of the sons of the deceased original defendant, in his deposition denied alleged oral gift, DW 2 Joynal Abedin and DW 3 Abdul Matin testified that the deceased defendant's relationship with the appellant was not cordial, but strained. 

 11. For a valid Mohammedan gift there must be (1) declaration of gift by the donor, (2) an acceptance of the gift expressed or implied by or on behalf of the donee and (3) delivery of possession of the subject of gift by the donor to the donee, In case of non-fulfillment of anyone of the above three conditions the gift will be invalid, In the instant case there is neither assertion in the plaint nor any evidence that the appellant ever accepted the alleged gift in any manner, There is also no evidence in support of delivery of possession. As found above the appellant never exercised her right as owner of the suit building on the basis of the alleged gift. She used to live there as the wife of its owner and has been continuing to live there even after divorce. Thus the alleged oral gift and appellant's right, title and interest in the suit property on the basis of such gift had not been proved. 

 13. On the above reasons we find that the appellant miserably failed to prove alleged oral gift and consequentially her right, title and interest in the suit property. Therefore, the trial Court rightly and legally dismissed the suit. The appeal, having no merit, fails.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Syed Muhammad Dastagir Husain

parties:
The People's Republic, of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary Ministry of Works, Bangladesh Secretariat Building, Dhaka ----- Appellant
Vs. 
The Chairman, 1st Court of Settlement, Dhaka and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Hamidul Haque, J:- This appeal has been filed against the judgment and order dated 27.10.1997 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 1370 of 1994. Leave was granted by the order-dated 9.8.2000 to consider the question whether the decree obtained by respondent No. 2 in a suit for specific performance of contract in respect of a property which has been enlisted as an abandoned property in the "Ka" list is a bar for inclusion of such property as an abandoned property and whether the High Court Division misdirected itself in law in deciding the writ petition in not considering the question that the onus to prove that the property in question was not an abandoned property was squarely upon the claimant and the government had no obligation to disclose the basis of treating the property as an abandoned property. Leave was also granted to consider whether the High Court Division fell into an error in holding that the property in question was not an abandoned property without giving any finding as to whether the original owner was present in Bangladesh or his whereabouts were known when the President's Order 16 of 1972 was promulgated. 

 2. Respondent No. 2, Md. Ziaul Islam filed an application under section 7 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 for exclusion of House No. 5/23, Block-D, Nurjahan Road, Mohammadpur from the "Ka" list of abandoned buildings published on 23.9.1986 in the official gazette. Md. Ziaul Islam claimed that Mustafa Ashraf took lease of the house property from the government of the then East Pakistan on the basis lease deed dated 27.7.1960 but subsequently by two agreements dated 28.7.1968 and 6.2.70, the original allottee entered into a contract with him for selling the house to him. He further claimed that possession was delivered to him by the original allottee on the basis of that agreement. Md. Ziaul Islam, further claimed that he filed a suit for specific performance of contract (Title Suit No. 12 of 1975) against the original allotee and in that suit the Government of Bangladesh was also defendant. The suit was decreed and on execution of the decree, he got a kabala through the court. Considering all the facts and circumstances specially considering the fact that the petitioner of the case i.e. Md. Ziaul Islam was able to prove his title and possession in the case property, the court of settlement declared that the case property was not abandoned property. Thereafter, Writ Petition No. 1370 of 1994 was filed on behalf of the People's Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works challenging the judgment and order passed by the 1st Court of settlement. The High Court Division after elaborate discussion found that there was no illegality in the impugned judgment of the Court of settlement and accordingly, the Rule was discharged by the High Court Division. 

 3. Mr. Abdur Razaque Khan, the learned Additional Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the appellant confined his argument mainly on one point. He has argued that before the Court of Settlement, Md. Ziaul Islam could not prove his possession in the property in question and the Court of settlement erroneously arrived at a finding that the petitioner proved his possession. Mr. Abdur Razaque Khan, clarified his argument by saying that the Court of settlement and also the High Court Division believed the claim of the petitioner's possession relying on the deeds of agreement. Then after taking us through the two deeds of agreement, he has submitted that in the deed of 1968 there is nothing to show that possession was delivered to Md. Ziaul Islam by the original allotee. Further, he has submitted that in the deed of agreement of 1970, only it is mentioned that Md. Ziaul Islam was inducted into possession. Mr. Abdur Razaque Khan has pointed out that no date of induction into possession is mentioned in the deed of 1970. 

 4. Mr. Mahmudul Islam the senior counsel who appeared for respondent no. 2, Md. Ziaul Islam, has submitted that in part performance of contract under section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, possession was delivered to the respondent No. 2 by the original allotee before date of execution of the second bainapatra, which was executed on 6.2.1970. He has further submitted that there was no material either before the Court of settlement or before the High Court Division to disbelieve the claim of delivering possession to the respondent No. 2 by the original allotee. 

 5. Mr. Abdur Razaque Khan, however, has argued that the Court of settlement ought to have made proper inquiry to ascertain whether the petitioner of the case Was in possession or some one else in possession of the case property. Mr. Abdur Razaque Khan has invited our attention to the additional paper book and submitted that one Tariqul Islam was actually in possession of House No. 5/23, Block-D, Nurjahan Road, Mohammadpur. The present appellant was a party in the Title Suit No. 12 of 1975, which was filed by the respondent No. 2 for a decree for specific performance of contract. The appellant was also party in the case filed before the Court of settlement and also in the writ petition. The appellant had the opportunity to produce relevant papers to show that Md. Ziaul Islam was not actually in possession of the case property. The question that Md. Ziaul Islam was not in possession of the case property having been raised for the first time before this Court, there is no scope of considering this question at this stage by this Court. 

 6. However, we have considered the argument of Mr. Abdur Razaque Khan that the Court of settlement ought to have made proper inquiry. Mr. Abdur Razaque Khan has pointed out that the Court of settlement relied on the deeds of agreement and those were not sufficient to arrive at a conclusion that the petitioner was in possession. Power and procedure of the Court of settlement is laid down in section 10 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985. Sub-section (5) of section 10 provides that a Court of settlement shall, after such inquiry as it may deem necessary and after giving reasonable opportunity to the parties concerned of being heard and also adducing evidence, both oral and documentary, may make such decision as it deems fit. In the instant case, the Court of settlement made inquiry to ascertain genuineness of the deeds of agreement. The Court of settlement called for the relevant file of Housing and Settlement Department and found that the signature of the original allotee found in that file tally with the signatures as contained in the bainapatras. In this way the Court of settlement, after being satisfied about the genuineness of bainapatra, came to the finding that the respondent No. 2 proved his title and possession in the case property. 

 7. The High Court Division also made elaborate discussion on the question of possession and arrived at the finding that the respondent No. 2 (the petitioner before the court of settlement) was in possession on the basis of the deeds of agreement. We find no illegality in the findings of the Court of Settlement or of the High Court Division on the question of possession. We have perused the principle laid down in the case of Buxly Paints Limited -Vs- Bangladesh reported in 31 DLR(AD) 266 and Bangladesh -Vs- K.M. Zakir Hossain reported in 8 BLC(AD) 27. In the above two cases question arose as to the right of a person in possession of the abandoned property on the basis of agreement for sale and it has been decided that such property cannot be taken over as an abandoned property. The respondent No. 2 claimed his possession in the property on the basis of two deeds of agreement, which were executed in 1968 and 1970, that is, both the deeds were executed prior to the war of liberation. The appellant could not produce any material to disbelieve the possession of the respondent No. 2 which he claimed on the basis of the deeds of agreement. There is also nothing on record to show that possession was taken over from the respondent No. 2 so as to list the building in "Ka" list. In view of the fact that the respondent No. 2 came into possession at least in the year 1970 when the second deed of agreement was executed, the question whether the original owner was present in Bangladesh when the Presidents Order No. 16 of 1972 was promulgated is not at all relevant. The respondent No. 2 made the prayer for exclusion of the case property from "Ka" list not on the basis of a decree which he obtained in the suit for specific performance of contract but on the basis of the deeds of agreement and claimed that he had been in possession from before promulgation of the President Order 16 of 1972. When his possession in the case property has been proved or the basis of the deeds of agreement, the last one being executed in February, 1970, there is no scope of enlisting the case property in the "Ka" list as abandoned property. We find no infirmity in the judgment and order passed by the court of settlement or by the High Court Division in the Writ Petition No. 1370 of 1994.

caseno:
Civil Revision Case No. 264 of 2000 
with 
Civil Revision Case No. 2588 of 1999
parties:
Kajol Das and others ------ Petitioners
vs.
Manowara Begum alias Marium Begum and ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. The short facts for disposal of the Rule in Civil Revision No. 264 of 2000 are that the petitioner as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 for Specific Performance of Contract in respect of schedule property against the defendants-opposite parties 1-10, stating, in short, that the land under District Dhaka PS Demra Mouja Tara Bari, CS Khatian No. 306 CS Plot No. 647 1.04 acres land in which 0.02 acres was owned and possessed by late Mosleuddin by inheritance, the predecessor of opposite party Nos. 1-9 who executed a Bainapatra on 3-11-82 with the plaintiff-petitioner for sale of 0134 ajusangsha on consideration of value at Taka 13,000 out of which he paid Taka 3000 and the seller handed over vacant possession and thereafter, plaintiff filled up null land by earth and built a chapra house thereon by investing huge sum of money and leased the house on rent to one Md Hafiz on oral agreement and thereafter executed written agreement on 1-3-93 and that the predecessor of defendants as well as they refused to execute sale deed and lodged a complaint by wife of late Moslehuddin before Commissioner who on hearing both the parties directed defendants predecessor to execute sale deed in favour of plaintiff on 18-1-83 and thereafter predecessors of defendant died leaving successors defendant Nos. 1-9 who also avoided to execute sale deed and defendant No. 1 again lodged complaint against husband of plaintiff before the present Ward Commissioner who notified both the parties and upon hearing on 1-5-97 delivered judgment directing the defendants 1-9 to execute sale deed by taking rest dues of Taka 10,000 which was not complied with and defendants issued a legal notice under section 106 of TP Act for eviction and plaintiff replied to the same and filed the suit for Specific Performance of Contract. 

 3. The opposite party Nos. 1-9 as defendants contested the suit and filed written statement, moreover, they filed SCC Suit No. 16/97 for eviction denying the material allegations of the plaint of the said Title Suit. 

 5. The learned trial Court decreed the Suit in favour of the plaintiff, and defendants preferred Title Appeal No. 461 of 1998 before District Judge, Dhaka who transferred the same to First Sub-Judge, Dhaka for disposal who allowed the appeal dismissing the suit and decreed the SCC Suit. The opposite parties filed Civil Revision No. 2588 of 1999 against the said judgment of SCC Suit which is being heard analogously with Civil Revision No. 264 of 2000. 

 6. The short facts for disposal of Rule in Civil Revision No. 2588 of 1999 is that the defendant-opposite party (plaintiff in said Title Suit No. 243 of 97) took lease of the demised premises measuring 0.02 acres of vacant land on 1.2.83 from Mosleuddin (plaintiff No. 2, husband and father of rest plaintiffs) in presence of Ramijuddin, Abdul Hoshem, Dukhu Mia and other elites of the locality. Oral agreement of lease was made and it was stipulated that the defendant (plaintiff in Title Suit No. 243 of 1997) would construct a tin shed house at his own cost and deal in sanitary business therein, electric bill, holding tax to be paid by the tenant defendant in the name of the plaintiffs predecessor Mosleuddin, the owner landlord, of the case premises, but at the ill advice and instigation of the unscrupulous people of the locality with a view to grabbing the schedule premises on 10-1-83 the defendant and his accomplices confined the mentally retarded person (the predecessor of the plaintiffs) Mosleuddin in a place and took signatures on some unwritten stamp papers, on the next day of the incident the said Musleuddin through his son plaintiff No. 2 made a General Diary with the Local Thana dated 11-1-1983 (Exhibit Gha) and subsequently, Mosleuddin died on 22-5-84 in the Dhaka Medical College Hospital, the defendant paid rents upto May 1999 at the rate of Taka 500 per month according to stipulation, but the defendant defaulted payment of rent since June, 1997 in spite of repeated demands and takids of the plaintiffs and lastly, the defendant denied the ownership of the plaintiffs refusing payment of further rents, the defendant on 25-5-1977 tried to forcibly construct a tin shed and the matter was brought to the local Commissioner who served a notice for stopping construction work and GD Entry on 26-5-97 was made in the local thana, the premises in Schedule is bonafide required for use and occupation of the plaintiff and for development of case property, the defendant has become defaulter and that is why a legal notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was served upon the defendant determining the tenancy and for realisation of arrear rent, on receipt of notice by the said defendant the defendant hurriedly instituted Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 on 21-8-97 in the 6th Court of Assistant Judge for specific performance of contract in the name of his wife. 

 7. The defendant contested the said suit by filing a written statement stating the plaint case of Title Suit No. 243 of 1997. 

 9. The learned trial Court decreed Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 and dismissed SCC Suit No. 16 of 1997 by the judgment and decree dated 29-10-98. As against that the defendants in Title Suit No. 243 of 97 preferred Title Appeal No. 461 of 1998 and the learned appellate Court vide his judgment and decree dated 11-7-99 allowed the appeal. 

 11. Mr Abdul Quayyum with Mr Tapas Kumar Das, Advocates appearing on behalf of the petitioners in both the Rules, placed both the revisional applications,  impugned judgments and decrees passed by the Courts below. At the time of hearing of the revisional applications the petitioners in Civil Revision 264 of 2000 filed an application for amendment of the plaint, the copy of which was served on the learned Advocate of the opposite parties. It has been stated in the said application that plaintiff-petitioner since dead being in possession of the suit land since date of agreement dated 3-1-82, he acquired good title in the Suit land by adverse possession and that he is entitled to relief for continuation of possession and permanent injunction and, as such, he prayed for adding a relief No. Kha in the prayer portion of the plaint to the effect that, 

 12. The learned Advocate for the petitioner also submitted that the original plaintiff being in possession of the Suit land since date of agreement dated 3-11-82 and he having filed the suit on 21-8-97 the plaintiff and his heirs the petitioners acquired good title in the Suit land by adverse possession and, as such, entitled to get a decree at least for confirmation of possession as well as permanent injunction. The learned Advocate further submitted that in view of the decision in the case of Md Nurul Islam Patwari and others vs Abdul Awal Mia and others reported in 1996 BLD (AD) 169 there is no bar in allowing the amendment as prayed for before this Court. 

 14. On perusal of the judgment it appears that the learned trial Court held that the suit is maintainable, that there is no defect of parties in Title Suit No. 243 of 1997, that the Suit is not barred, that the deed of agreement dated 3-11-82 has been duly executed by Mosleuddin, predecessor of the defendants, that the allegation by the defendants that the signatures of said Mosleuddin was obtained by force in blank stamp papers is not believable, that plaintiff is in possession of the Suit land since the date of the deed of agreement dated 3-11-82, that the defendants failed to prove that Ratan Das, husband of the plaintiff, is a monthly tenant under the defendants, that the SCC Suit No. 16 of 1997 is a counter-case of Title Suit No. 243 of 1997. On those findings the learned trial Court decreed the Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 and dismissed SCC Suit No. 16 of 1997. 

 15. The learned appellate Court, on the other hand, held that Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 is barred by limitation inasmuch as the plaintiff failed to prove the cause of action and accordingly, allowed the appeal dismissing Title Suit No. 243 of 1997. 

 16. Admittedly the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 is in possession of the suit land and the defendant of that suit as plaintiff filed SCC Suit No. 16 of 1997 for eviction of the plaintiff alleging that he the defendant of SCC suit is a monthly bharatia and he is a habitual defaulter, The trial Court specifically found that the plaintiff is in possession of the Suit land since the date of agreement dated 3-11-82 but the learned appellate Court did not give any finding as to the date of possession of the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 243 of 1997. The plaintiff in the SCC Suit stated that the defendant in the SCC suit took lease of the Suit land with effect from 1-1-83 and the defendant paid rent upto May, 1997 @ Taka 500 per month and that subsequently, the defendant defaulted in payment of rent since June 1997, necessitating the filing of the Suit for ejectment. Thus it shows that that the defendant in the SCC Suit who is the plaintiff is Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 is in possession of the Suit land according to the plaintiff with effect from 3-11-82 and according to the defendant with effect from 1-1-83 which shows that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land for more than 12 years when the present suit was filed on 21-8-97. The case of the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 is that on the basis of the agreement dated 3-11-82 she is in possession of the Suit land. Since the learned trial Court decreed the suit but the learned appellate Court allowed the appeal holding that the plaintiff could not prove her cause of action for the Suit and accordingly, the Suit is barred by limitation as she failed to file the suit within 3 years from the date of cause of action as alleged by the plaintiff. 

 20. On perusal of the said decision, it appears that in a similar case application for amendment of the plaint was allowed wherein a suit for declaration of title by adverse possession was filed by the plaintiff and the defendant of the said suit also filed a SCC Suit for eviction of the plaintiff. In the said reported case, the original suit was for declaration of title by adverse possession on the basis of an agreement and subsequently, by amendment at the revisional stage the Suit was converted to a Suit for permanent injunction upon confirmation of possession and ultimately, in the said reported case the Suit was decreed which was affirmed upon the Appellate Division. Thus, in my opinion, the aforesaid decision reported in 1996 BLD is equally applicable in the present case as the facts and circumstances are similar to those of the reported case and accordingly, the amendment as prayed for by this petitioner in Civil Revision 264 of 2000 is allowed. 

 21. Since I have found as above the plaintiff in Civil Revision 264 of 2000 has been able to prove her possession in the suit land for more than 12 years, in my opinion she acquired a good title by adverse possession and she is entitled to get a decree in Title Suit No. 243 of 1997. 

 22. Since it has been found by the trial Court that the present plaintiff in Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 is in possession of the suit land by virtue of the agreement dated 3-11-82 and she or her husband is not a tenant of the (defendant in Title Suit No. 243 of 1997) plaintiff in SCC Suit No. 16 of 1997 said suit cannot be decreed and the learned appellate Court committed error in decreeing SCC Suit No. 16 of 1997 calling for interference by this Court. 

 23. For the aforesaid discussions and reasons the Rule in 264 of 2000 is made absolute without any order as to cost and the judgment and decree dated 11-7-99 passed by the learned appellate Court in Title Appeal No. 461 of 1998 are set aside and those of the learned trial Court are restored but decree in modified form as per amendment of the plaint as stated above, i.e. Title Suit No. 243 of 1997 is decreed and the defendants are restrained permanently from disturbing the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs in the Suit land. Consequently, the Rule in Civil Revision No. 2588 of 1999 is discharged without cost and those passed by the learned trial Court in SCC Suit No. 16 of 1997 are maintained. The order of status quo granted at the time of issuance of the Rule in Civil Revision No. 264 of 2000 is vacated.

parties:
Mujibul Haque ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Lokman Mia ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The review petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 176 of 1984 in the Court of Upazila Munsif, Begumganj for declaration of his title to. 19 acres of suit land with prayer for injunction restraining the Government from leasing out .08 acres of his share of the suit tank to the defendant appellant respondent Lokman Mia, restraining him from disturbing his possession of the suit tank and for partition of the suit land. His case is that the Government of India acquired entire land of C. S. Plot No. 21 which originally belonged to one Aslam Mia and land of others under the land Acquisition Act. 1894 during 1940-41 for the purpose of establishing the district headquarters of Noakhali, but the government never took possession of the acquired lands and he purchased the suit land from the admitted owner by three registered kabalas dated 24.3.74 and 24.12.77. Since then he has been in possession of the suit land and the Government was now contemplating to lease out the same including the suit tank to the respondent. The respondents contested the suit by filing written statements stating inter alia that the appellant did not acquire any title to the suit land by purchase as the suit land was acquired and there by the title vested in the government. The trial court decreed the suit. 

 3. The respondent Lokman Mia filed Title Appeal No. 101 of 1988 and the Government respondent filed Cross Appeal No. 128 of 1988. The appeals were heard together by the lower appellate court which allowed the appeals setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial court dismissing the suit. The respondent, against the decree of the lower appellate court, filed Civil Revision NO. 5089 of 1991 and the same was made absolute by the learned Single Judge by the judgment and order dated 19.3.1997. 

 4. Being aggrieved the respondent filed Civil Appeal No. 76 of 1997 before this Division which allowed. This Division found that the High court Division had committed an error in misapplying section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act 1894 by holding therefore, the suit land has not yet been vested absolutely in the Government and the plaintiff can hold the suit land till the Government takes possession thereof in accordance with law. On perusal of the judgment passed by the learned District Judge we find that he did not consider the case in this aspect and consequently he has committed an error of law resulting error in his decision occasioning failure of justice. "This Division held that this was an erroneous view of the law by the learned Judge of the High Court Division. A careful reading of section 16 indicates that where the collector has made an I award under Section 11 in respect of land acquired under this Act such land shall vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances. Thus, vesting title in the land acquired becomes absolute as soon as compensation award is made. If the Government after making compensation award does not elect to go physically into possession of land, it cannot be said that because of that title does not vest absolutely in the government. According to Section 16 vesting is absolute as soon as commendation award is made. This view was also expressed in the case of Bangladesh vs. Barekunnessa 4 BLC (AD) (1999) 130, In the instant case it was evidently found by the Court below that compensation money was deposited in the Civil deposit which sufficiently indicates that award was made by the Collector in terms of Section 11 of the Act. Further the plaintiff without challenging the validity or otherwise of the acquisition proceeding challenged the right of the Government to lease out the suit land on the ground that he was in possession by purchase from the original owner and sought for declaration of his title to the suit land. It also appears that the suit land along with other land was recorded in the Government Khas Khatain No. 1 in 1960 and the Court of appeal below reversed the finding of the trial court that Government received rents from the original owner as the some is based on no evidence and this has not been reversed by the High court Division. Accordingly this Division held that the High Court Division in revision committed an illegality in setting aside the judgment of the lower appellate court. 

 5. It is now submitted by the plaintiff review petitioner that in the meantime he has come to know from Serajuddin Ahmed one of the heirs of the recorded tenant Md. Musa Mia that the suit property was never acquired by the Government and as such the Title Suit No. 176 of 1984 in the Court of Upazial Munsif, Begumgaj filed by the petitioner was in wrong forum and as such a review is justifiable in this appeal. It is also submitted that the petitioner made a search in the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali as to whether the suit land or its portion was acquired at all by the Government. The office of the Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali on 31.1.2001 replied to that the Government did not acquire the aforesaid suit land or any portion of it. It is further submitted that the petitioner of the aforesaid Title Suit No. 176 of 1984 due to mistaken belief had wrongly described the suit land as acquired by the government. 

 These submissions were never made at any stage in disposing of the title Suit No. 176 of 1984. The petitioner is now making out a third case with completely now facts which cannot be considered and decided in review.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 525 of 2000
parties:
Kartic Chandra Sarker being dead his heirs Samiran Sarker and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Anarathi Mondal and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Syed JR Mudassir Husain J: The petitioners, the substituted heirs of original defendant N6. 1 Kartic Chandra Sarker, are seeking leave to appeal against the judgment and order dated 19-1-2000 passed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division making the Rule absolute in Civil Revision No. 449 of 1992. 

 2. The plaintiff-respondent No. 1 Srimati Anarathi Mondal instituted Title Suit No. 73 of 1983 on 2-3-1983 in the Court of Munsif now Assistant Judge, Khulna against the said defendant No. 1 and others praying for a declaration that the compromise decree dated 21-6-1962 passed in the earlier Title Suit No. 182 of 1962 of the 1st Court of Munsif, Khulna filed by the said defendant No. 1 against the respondent No. 1 is forged, fraudulent, collusive and not binding upon her (respondent No. 1) stating to the effect that the suit land belonged to her father Bisturam Gain and RS and SA Khatian were correctly recorded in her father's name; that the said defendant No. 1 Kartic Chandra Sarker was a village quack and a litigant person of the locality. The plaintiffs father died leaving behind her as only daughter and 3 grandsons to inherit properties left by said Bishuram; that plaintiff possessed the suit land on payment of rent. But when the plaintiffs son Bimal went to pay rent in the year 1983 he was surprised to see the name of Kartic Chandra Sarker defendant No. 1 in the record of right in place of her father Bisturam Gain; that on an inquiry it was detected that said defendant No.1 mutated his name in Miscellaneous Case No. 22 of 1978-79 on the basis of a compromise decree dated 21-6-1962 passed in Title Suit No. 182 of 1962. Against the present respondent No. 1; that plaintiff respondent never received any summons or notice as defendant and she did not compromise the suit by putting her thumb impression in any application of compromise. The alleged compromise decree was obtained by practicing fraud. The defendant No. 1 contested the instant suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations contending, inter alia, that the suit land belonged to Bisturam Gain, father of the respondent No. 1. But said Bisturam settled the suit land orally to him (defendant No. 1) and subsequently, granted an 'Amalnama' in Jaistha 1356 BS; that Bisturam also granted him rent receipt and delivered possession of the suit land. During SA operation the name of Bisturam was wrongly recorded in the SA Khatian and the plaintiff respondent as daughter of Bisturam was claiming the suit land and, as such, the said defendant No. 1 (predecessor of leave-petitioners) had to file Title Suit No. 182 of 1962 and that suit was compromised between the respondent No. 1 and the defendant No. 1 (predecessor of the present petitioners). The compromise was genuine and defendant No. 1 has been in possession of the suit land for long over 12 years and thereby acquired a valid title in the suit land. 

 3. The learned Munsif by his judgment and decree dated 14-12-1988 decreed the suit in favour of the respondent No. 1 and against which the defendant No. 1 (the predecessor of the present leave-petitioners) filed Title Appeal No. 26 of 1989 and the appellate Court allowed the same by dismissing the suit. The plaintiff respondent then moved the High Court Division in revision and the Rule obtained was made absolute by the impugned judgment of the High Court Division. 

 4. Mr. Nowab Ali; the learned Advocate-on-Record, placed before us the judgments of the courts below and then submitted that the learned Single Judge misread and misdirected himself in not adverting to definite finding of the appellate Court to the effect that the 'Left Thumb Impression' (LTI) of the plaintiff, appearing on the petition of compromise filed along with two other defendants, in the previous Title Suit No. 182 of 1962 of defendant was endorsed by her husband Paresh Nath Mondal himself under his signature, who being alive was not examined as a witness in the instant suit for setting aside the compromise decree in the previous Title Suit No. 182 of 1962 and, as such, the initial onus to prove that the plaintiff did not put her left thumb impression on the petition of compromise in that suit was not at all discharged by the respondent No. 1 herein and thus the onus to disprove the plaintiffs case did not absolutely shift to the present defendant No. 1 on mere denial. The High Court Division having not considered this aspect committed error of law resulting in an error in the decision causing failure of justice. 

 5. It has been further argued that the High Court Division committed an error of law in holding that summons of Title Suit No. 182 of 1962 was not served upon the plaintiff respondent No. 1 as defendant of that suit although there was a definite finding of the Appellate Court that summons were served upon her and, as such, judgment passed by the High Court Division is not a proper judgment of reversal. It is also argued that the learned Single Judge also failed to consider the question of limitation involved in a suit for setting aside the compromise decree in the backdrop of legal presumption that all official acts were done correctly, that the plaintiff failed to produce any evidence of possession of the suit land for more than 41 (forty-one) years. 

 6. We have perused the judgments of the courts below including the impugned judgment of the High Court Division. It appears that the High Court Division in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction considered that the trial Court on consideration and assessment of evidence on record found that the plaintiff (respondent No. 1) has correctly asserted that the summons of earlier suit No. 182 of 1962 filed by original defendant was not served and the 'soleh' decree was obtained by practicing fraud and collusion. 

 7. It appears that when the plaintiff respondent No. 1 disowned her thumb impression appearing in the alleged 'solenama' it was incumbent upon the original defendant, the predecessor of the leave-petitioners, to prove the thumb impression of the plaintiff respondent No. 1 by obtaining an expert opinion. The trial Court considered this aspect but the lower appellate Court as a final court of fact failed to consider the same and in such view of the matter we hold that the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division having legally considered all aspects of the case based on material evidence on record rightly set aside the judgment of the lower appellate Court. We find no illegality has been committed by the High Court Division. The High Court also noticed that the plaintiff respondent No. 1 asserted that no summons of Title Suit No. 182 of 1962 filed by the original defendant No. 1 were served upon her and by this assertion of denial the onus has thus then shifted to the original defendant No. 1 (predecessor of the petitioners) and it was then incumbent upon him (defendant No. 1) to rebut the plaintiffs' said assertion by cogent evidence on record. The learned Single Judge, in our view, has rightly held to the effect that in the facts and circumstances of the case the onus shifted on the defendant No. 1 to show that the summons of the earlier suit was served on the plaintiff. This will not be enough and the defendant will have to further prove that the 'Soleh' decree was not obtained by practicing fraud and collusion.
