2. The prosecution case, in short, is that accused appellant Md. Sirajuddin Sheikh and his brother co-accused Abul Mansur Sheikh on 25,5.91 filed a case before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.), Gazipur for mutation in their names land measuring 37.90 acres appertaining to the Government khas khatian of Mouza Pelayet, Police Station Sreepur, District Gazipur, on the basis of a decree allegedly passed in their favour in Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 passed by the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Gazipur wherein their title was declared. The application for mutation created suspicion in the mind of the Revenue Officer who enquired into the matter personally in the office of the Subordinate Judge, Gazipur and came to learn that the aforesaid Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 of the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Gazipur was dismissed on 27.11.90 on contest against the plaintiffs and their claim of a decree in that suit was totally false and fraudulent. Thereafter the Assistant Commissioner of Land at Gazipur lodged a complainant at Gazipur Police Station against the accused appellant and his brother Abul Hossain Sheikh for creating a false and fictitious certified copy of the judgment in respect of Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 of the Court of the Subordinate Judge. Gazipur and use the said false and forged certified copy in the mutation proceedings before the Revenue Officer, Gazipur. The report of the Revenue Officer containing the aforesaid allegations has been treated as the FIR in the case and marked as Ext. 14. 

 11. P.W. 1 Mr. M. A. Baset, is the Sheristadar of the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Gazipur. He stated in his evidence that on 28.11.90 he was the chief comparer of the copying section of the Court. He stated that Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 (in which accused appellant Md. 

 Sirajuddin Sheikh and his brother co-accused Abul Mansur Sheikh were the plaintiffs) was dismissed on contest on 27.11.90. He also stated that there was no interpolation or erasures anywhere in the original copy of the judgment of the aforesaid Title Suit no. 72 of 1988. He went on to state that subsequently the judgment of the said Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 was seized by the police and preparing a seizure list in Ext. 1. His signature in Ext. 1 has been marked as Ext. 1/ka. He further stated that if any erasures or interpolations are found anywhere in a judgment, the matter is instantaneously brought to the notice of the Presiding Officer of the Court by the 

 office of the District Judge, Gazipur. She stated in her evidence that on 28.11.90 she was attached to the copying department. She, of course, pleaded her ignorance about Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 of the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Gazipur. 

 judgment and decree of Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 of the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Gazipur. 

 Station. On 6.8.92 he was attached to Joydebpur Police Station and he was given the charge of investigation of the case. He stated in his evidence that he sent a letter of request to the Bureau of Anti-Corruption to expedite the investigation of the case. This letter has been marked as Ext. 2 and his signature therein has been marked as Ext. 2/ka. P.W. 8 he is an office Assistant of the District Bureau of Anti-Corruption, Gazipur. He stated in his evidence that on 13.1.93 the police seized from accused Sirajuddin a copy of the judgment of Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 marked Ext 11 and his signature therein has been marked as Ext. 11/ka. In cross-examination he stated that he could not say if Ext-11 was recovered from the pocket of accused Sirajuddin. 

 19. P.W.9 Assistant Inspector Mojibur Rahman is attached to the Bureau of District Anti-Corruption, Gazipur. He stated in his evidence that he seized on 1.12.92 the order sheet of Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 of the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Gazipur. The order dated 17.11.90 has been marked as Ext-3, the judgment and decree of the said suit have been marked as Exts 4 and 5 respectively. He also seized the final order of the said suit Ext-6. the Daily Roster Ext-7 and the Daily Cause list Ext-8 and the application of the advocate's clerk Ext-9 on preparing seizure list marked Ext-10. His signature in Ext-10 has been marked as Ext-10/ka. He stated that the Suit Register was left in the jimma of the court. He further stated that on 13.1.93 he seized from accused appellant Sirajuddin the attested copy of the judgment of Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 of the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Gazipur named Ext- II which 12 contains his signature, marked Ext.-11 /ka. He stated that it has been written in Ext-10, the attested copy of the judgment of Title Suit No. 72 of 1988, that the suit has been decreed in favour of the plaintiffs. 

 20. P.W. 10 M. Hassan Imam had been the Subordinate Judge of Gazipur from 29.9.89 to 18.6.92. He stated in his evidence that during the incumbency of his office at Gazipur he delivered the judgment in Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 on 27.11.90 and the suit was dismissed on contest. He further stated that accused Sirajuddin Sheikh and another were the plaintiffs of that suit, which was dismissed on contest with cost. He also stated that it has been clearly noted in order No. 2 of the order sheet that Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 has been dismissed on contest against the plaintiffs. Order-28 of the order sheet of the suit has been marked as Ext-13 and the signature of the witness therein has been marked as Ext-13/ka. He stoutly denied the defence suggestion that he cannot say if the suit was decreed or dismissed. 

 21. P.W. 11 Mr. Md. Nuruzzaman is the Senior Assistant Secretary, E.R.D. Government of Bangladesh. He stated in his evidence that on 10.1.93 he took up the investigation of the case, visited the place of occurrence, examined witnesses and recorded their statements under section-161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, seized alamats as per seizure list Ext. His signature in Ext-1 has been marked as Ext-I. /ka. He submitted before the Court the original copy of the judgment delivered on 27.11.90 by the learned Subordinate Judge Gazipur in T,S. No. 72 of 1988, marked Ext-4. The original decree of the aforesaid suit has been marked as Ext-5 while the order sheet of the aforesaid suit has been marked as Ext-6. No also proved the signatures of the learned Subordinate Judge in Exts. 4 and 5 and 6. On completion of the investigation. he submitted charge sheet against the accused persons on obtaining sanction for their prosecution from the appropriate authority. 

 22. In cross-examination he stated that the certified copy of the judgment of Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 could not be recovered. He stated that he seized the attested copy of the judgment of Title Suit No. 72 of 1988, which was attested by a Magistrate of the 1st Class, from accused Sirajuddin. In answer to a question put to him by the Court, the witness clearly stated that accused Sirajuddin had supplied to him the disputed attested copy of the judgment of Title Suit No. 72 of 1988. 

 26. From the evidence discussed above, the learned Special Judge found that accused appellant Md. Sirajuddin Sheikh by restarting to forgery and fabrication of the false and fictitious attested copy of the judgment allegedly delivered on 27.11.90 by the learned Subordinate Judge, Gazipur he tried to change the result of the said suit by showing that the suit was decreed in their favour, although, in fact, the suit was dismissed on contest against them. It has also been found that the accused appellant by fabricating a. false and fictitious attested copy of the judgment of the aforesaid Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 of the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Gazipur filed an application for mutation of their names in respect of the suit property by using a false  and forged certified copy of the judgment. The I.O. of the case seized the so-called attested copy of the judgment of the aforesaid Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 froth accused appellant Md. Sirajuddin Sheikh as per seizure list Ext. 12. The forged and fabricated attested copy of the judgment of Title Suit No. 72 of 1988, seized from accused appellant Sirajuddin Sheikh, has been marked as Ext-11. In the facts of the case, it is evident that accused appellant Sirajuddin Sk. and his brother Mansur Sk., since acquitted, by creating a false and fabricated copy of the judgment of Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 used. The same in their bid to mutatate their names in a mutation proceeding before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Gazipur for illegaly grabbing 37.90 acres of Government Khas land. It is manifestly evident that accused appellant. Sirajuddin Sheikh and his brother Abdul Mansur Sheikh are the sole beneficiaries of the fictitious and fabri-cated copy of the judgment of Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 (Ext-11) and they consciously used it for reaping the full benefits of the false decree at the expenses of the Government. It is clearly found from the evidence of P.W. 11 Mr. Md. Nuruzzaman that this forged fictitious and fabricated copy of the judgment of Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 of the court of the Subordinate Judge, Gazipur was seized from accused Sirajuddin Sheikh. 

 27. P.W. 9 I.O. Mojibur Rahman also stated in his evidence that the forged and fictitious attested copy of the judgment of Title Suit No. 72 of 1988, marked Ext-1 I was seized on production of the same by accused appellant Md. Sirajuddin. This Ext-11 has been seized vide seizure list. Ext-12. Ext-11 appears to have been seized from accused appellant Sirajuddin Sk. in presence of two witnesses P.W.6 Md. Saidul Haque and P.W. 8 Nazimuddin. It is found from the case records that the records of Mutation Case No. 6-4/91 of the office of the A.D.C. (Rev.), Gazipur were also seized in connection with this case. In this case, accused appellant Sirajuddin Sk. and his brother Abul Mansur Sk. prayed for mutation of their names in respect of a vast tract of Govt. Khas land on 'the basis of a false and factious decree Ext-11 allegedly obtained in Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 of the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Gazipur. It is the prosecution case that Mrs. Namita Haider was the Revenue Deputy Collector at Gazipur at the relevant time and she took active interests in the case in detecting the acts of fraud and forgeries resorted to by the accused persons but she has not been examined in the case by the prosecution for unknown reasons. It is strange that P.W. 4 Mrs. Rokeya and P.W. 5 Humayun Kabir have been examined in the case in a most casual and irresponsible manner by an indifferent and incompetent prosecution. It is found from seizure list Ext. 12 that the so-called attested copy of the judgment of T. S. No. 72 of 1988 was seized by the I.O. from the accused appellant and this has been marked as Ext-11. The Ext-11 was seized in presence of witnesses namely P.W. 4 Mrs. Rokeya Begum and P.W. 8 Nizamuddin but unfortunately it has not been taken from them that this valuable document proving the guilt of the accused appellant was seized in their presence from the accused appellant. A totally callous and incompetent Public Prosecutor conducting the case did not even draw their attention to this valuable document which practically provides life-blood to the prosecution case. 

 that in the absence of any evidence from seizure list witnesses namely P.W. 4 Mrs. Rokeya Begum and P.W.8 Nazimuddin that this vital documentary evidence seizure list Ext-12, by which the incriminating attested copy of the disputed judgment Ext-11 was allegedly seized by the I.O. from accused Md. Sirajuddin Sheikh, it is wholly unsafe to pass an order of conviction and sentence on a charge of forgery. The conduct of the Investigation Officer is equally deplorable. Mrs. Namita Haider, the Revenue Deputy Collector of Gazipur at the relevant time and the person who took an active part in detecting the diabolical fraud has not even been made a witness in the case. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record, it appears that accused appellant Sirajuddin and his brother co-accused Abul Mansur Sk. created a false and factious attested copy of the judgment of Title Suit No. 72 of 1988 of the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Gazipur showing that the suit was decreed in their favour, although it was dismissed on con-test, and used the said document in a mutation proceeding before the A.D.C. (Rev.), Gazipur for laying a false claim upon about 40 acres of Government Khas land. To strengthen their false claim, they also tampered with official records of the case in a most ruthless and daredevil manner. Be that as it may, in the facts of the case, I think, it will be unsafe to sustain the order of conviction and sentence without giving a chance to the accused to cross-examine the witnesses in whose presence Ext-11 was seized by the I.O. vide seizure list Ext-12. The seizure list by which the I.O. seized the records of Mutation Case No. 6-4/91 containing the petition of accused appellant Md. Sirajuddin Sheikh and his brother co-accused Abul Mansur Sheikh does not appear to have been brought on record legally and marked exhibit in the case. 2. The short fact leading to this appeal is that respondent as plaintiff instituted Other Class Suit No. 70 of 1966 in the aforesaid court for declaration of title and recovery of possession of part of that suit land alleging that the jote comprising Plot Nos. 4653, 5321 and 2148 measuring 1.35 acres appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 280 of Mouza Goalgaon under Faridpur Police Station of the District of Pabna originally belonged to one Hridoy Nath Sarkar in jote right under landlord Ashutosh Sanyal. This jote was put to auction and the said landlord on 9.8.1936 auctioned purchased the same but before taking delivery of possession Hridoy Nath Sarkar approached the said landlord for re-settlement which was granted on 21st Baisak 1344 B.S. by an 'Amalnama' exhibit- 2 and after the death of Hridoy Nath Sarkar his son Kalipada Sarkar sold suit Plot No. 4653 on 2.9.1952 measuring .52 acres to respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and their brother Abul Kashem Khan who died on 2.3.1961 leaving behind two brothers and mother who are plaintiffs as his heirs. These two respondents sold their shares in the suit plot to their mother who thus by purchase as well as by inheritance got the entire suit land. That Rhidoy Nath Sarkar and his son Kalipada used to pay rent in the landlord Sherestha vide exhibit- 1 series and the original defendant Saimuddin Pramanik had no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land but by creating certain fake documents he illegally got the record in his name during S.A. operation in respect of the suit land along with other land which necessitated the plaintiff to 

 6. It appears that the trial court decreed the suit and declared title of the plaintiff over the suit land and also for recovery of khas possession from certain portion of the suit land from which the Plaintiffs were allegedly dispossessed during pendency of the suit. The appellate court it appears considered the documents of the plaintiff and came to the finding that the documents of the plaintiffs are all forged and fictitious documents on which the plaintiff cannot get the decree as prayed for. It also of course found that the documents of the defendants are also not legal documents. From consideration of the judgment of the High Court Division it appears that the High Court Division simply dismissed the evidence of the defence and finding fault dismissed the defence case and restored the decree passed by the trial court. Admittedly the suit land originally belonged to one Hridoy Nath Sarkar under landlord Ashutosh Sanyal and it is also an admitted fact that the suit jote was auction sold in 1936 and according to plaintiff Rhidoy Nath Sarkar took fresh settlement of the suit jote on 21st Baisak 1344 B.S. at a rental of Tk. 4.99 paisa on the basis of 'Amalnama' exhibit- 2 and entered into possession and continued to possess on payment of rent. The plaintiff produced Amalnama and Dakhilas which were exhibited before the trial court. These documents were in challenge by the defence. The appellate court it appears considered these documents particularly 'Amalnama' exhibit- 2 and came to the finding that these documents were not properly taken into evidence as P.W. 9 who came to prove the signature of Ashutosh Sanyal failed to do that. The appellate court found that she is not competent to know the signature as containing in exhibit-2 and the scribe of the 'Amalnama' exhibit-2 though was alive but he was not examined. So on consideration of these material evidence the appellate court found that the Amalnama and Dakhilas were not properly and legally proved and it found that. These documents have been created for the purpose of the suit. The appellate court also found that the dakhila exhibit.-1 series has no evidentiary value in view of non-examination of the scribe of the exhibits. The appellate court also found that there was no foundation that Rhidoy Nath Sarkar took settlement from Ashutosh after auction. So by subsequent purchase from the alleged tenant the plaintiff party acquired no title. The appellate court also found that the plaintiff failed to prove their possession in the suit property by examining reliable witnesses and there is no cause of action against recording of the land in the S.A. Khatian as alleged and when the onus of proving title and interest rests on the plaintiff they failed to discharge and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed. The appellate court also found the document of the defendant to be fabricated documents. 

 7. The High Court Division it appears has scrutinised the material documents of the defendant but has not thoroughly considered the documents produced by the plaintiff to prove their title and came to a wrong finding that the trial court rightly decreed the suit. There may be thousands of defects in the documents of the defence as well as their case but that does not entitle, the plaintiff to get a decree. The plaintiff is to prove his case irrespective of the defence version of the case and from the materials on record it appears that the plaintiff failed to prove genuineness of their documents and also their possession. This aspect of the matter escaped the notice of the High Court Division in the aforesaid Second Appeal and in such circumstances the finding of the High Court Division is wrong and cannot be sustained.

2. The short facts leading to this petition are that one Gouranga Chandra Dey who is respondent No. 1 earlier instituted Title Suit No. 68 of 1990 in the third Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for specific performance of contract against the predecessor of the petitioner. That suit was earlier dismissed, against which respondent No. I preferred Title Appeal No. 57 of 111 1977 before the lower appellate Court. The appellate Court set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and sent back the case on remand for fresh trial - Against that order of remand the present petitioner preferred Second Appeal No. 966 of 1978 before the High Court Division which was dismissed. Then the original .suit was taken up and re-numbered as Title Suit No. 68 of '1990 which was decreed ex parte in favour of respondent No. 1 who ultimately put the decree, into execution in Execution Case No. 18 of '1994 and got the sale deed which was registered. Thereafter the present petitioner filed Title Suit No. 244 of 1994 for a declaration that the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit. No. 68 of 1990 was illegal and void. In this suit an application was filed for rejection of the plaint under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure by respondent. No 1. After hearing the parties the trial Court rejected the plaint as prayed for and against that order of rejection of the plaint, First Appeal Tender No. 498 of 1998 has been filed by the Petitioner which is pending before the High Court Division. After filing of this First Appeal Tender the petitioner filed an application for slaying all further proceedings of Execution Case No. 18 of 1994 now pending before the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka and then the present Rule was issued and an ad interim order of stay was granted. Thereafter on hearing the learned Advocates of both sides the Division Bench of the High Court Division by judgment dated 17.5.1999 discharged the Rule. 

 3. Mr. Md. Fazlul Karim learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that though a sale deed was obtained and registered by respondent No. 1 in Execution Case No. 18 of 1994 this petitioner is still in possession grid as the suit he filed is for a declaration that the parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 68 of 19..)0 was illegal and void in all fairness pending proposal of First Anneal Tender No. 498 of 1998 of the High ct Division:1- further proceedings of the aforesaid execution case be stayed. 

 4. Admitted position is that In pursuance to the decree passed in Title Suit No. 68 of 1990 which was a suit for specific performance of contract, the plaintiff got the kabala executed and registered through Court and it appears that possession was also obtained in most of the suit land excepting of course a very small fraction of the land which is in possession of some unauthorised persons. The High Court Division found that since the decree has already been executed in Execution Case No. 18 of 1994 and the kabala has been registered on 20.10.1994 there is nothing to stay all further proceedings of the aforesaid execution case. The petitioner filed Title Suit No. 244 of 1994 for a declaration that the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 68 of 1990 was illegal and void which has nothing to do with the aforesaid execution proceeding and when the decree obtained by respondent No. I has already been executed, we are of the view that the High Court Division has not committed any wrong or illegality in refusing to stay further proceedings of aforesaid Execution Case No. 18 of 1994. Mr. Karim failed to make out any case for our interference in the matter. There is therefore no merit in this petition.

parties:
Mizanur Rahman Khan (Md) and another ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Jinnatul Ferdous and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the order dated 19-10-97 passed by the Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, 4th Court, Dhaka in Title Execution Case No. 20 of 1997 rejecting the application of the petitioners under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of possession on the ground that no executable decree was passed. 

 2. Short facts relevant for the purpose of the case are that, the predecessor-in-interest of opposite party Nos. 1-8 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 52 of 1986 under section 14 of the Arbitration Act to make the award dated 28-12-1985 rule of the Court. It has been stated that on the basis of an arbitration agreement dated 31-5-85 the parties appointed Mr. MA Rashid as the sole arbitrator to adjudicate the dispute in respect of the land mentioned in the agreement as to the shares of the parties thereto in the light of the different deeds of transfer. Reference was made to the arbitrator to ascertain the share of the four parties in the land under dispute whereupon the arbitrator ultimately made the following award: 

 1.	The first party is entitled to 0.4550 acre of land 

 2.	The 2nd party is entitled to 0.2250 acre of land 

 3.	The 3rd party is entitled to 0.2475 acre of land 

 4.	The 4th party is entitled to 0.4325 acre of land 

 3. Title Suit No. 52 of 1986 was originally filed in the 3rd Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka but subsequently it was transferred to the Court of the Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, 4th Court, Dhaka and it was renumbered as Title Suit No. 224 of 1992. The learned Subordinate Judge by his order dated 30-11-96 made the award the Rule of the Court on hearing the contending parties. 

 4. Thereafter opposite party Nos. 1-8 filed Title Execution Case No. 20 of 1997 in the Court of The Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No. 4, Dhaka praying for execution of the decree, following which the learned Executing Court appointed an Advocate Commissioner for the purpose and issued writ of delivery of possession to the Advocate Commissioner for execution of the award in 45-1/2 acre of unascertained land. It appears that in pursuance of the aforesaid writ the learned Advocate Commissioner along with a contingent of police force all on a sudden went to the spot on 18- 6-97 and on the showing of the petitioner forcibly evicted the petitioners' tenants who were living there and demolished the tin-shed structures. The learned Advocate Commissioner thereafter filed the report before the Court stating, inter alia, that he delivered possession to the petitioner of Title Execution Case No. 20 of 1997 in 18 acre of land but he could not deliver the - possession in the remaining portion of the suit property due to apprehension of tough resistance by the judgment- debtors and prayed for a larger contingent of police force for delivering possession to the decree-holder in the remaining portion of the suit property. It also appears that the present petitioners filed an application before the learned Execution Court under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for restoration of possession in the suit property from where they were allegedly dispossessed by the learned Advocate Commissioner. 

 5. The opposite parties contested the aforesaid application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure contending, inter alia, that the learned Executing Court rightly issued the writ of delivery of possession for giving physical possession of the suit property to the decree holder and the learned Advocate Commissioner in pursuance of the writ issued to him under Order 21 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure duly executed the writ and delivered possession to the decree-holder and, as such, the petitioners are not entitled to get any relief under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It was also contended that if any illegality was committed by the Executing Court, the petitioners had remedy before that Court but without availing the opportunity they are not entitled to invoke the application of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of possession and, as such, the application is liable to be rejected as being a misconceived one. 

 7. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that in view of the fact that the award, which was subsequently made Rule of the Court, merely determined the entitlement of the parties in respect of their shares in the disputed property without any reference to possession therein, the award decree are essentially a preliminary decree and it could not be executed without making the decree a final one in accordance with law and consequently all actions taken by the learned Advocate Commissioner in pursuance of the order of the Execution Court in forcibly evicting the petitioners' tenants from an unspecified portion of the suit property and demolition of the tin-sheds standing therein and delivering possession to the decree-holder are in clear violation of the provision of law and, as such, the petitioners are entitled under the law to restoration of possession in the suit property from where - they were illegally and arbitrarily dispossessed by the action of the Court. The learned Advocate for the petitioners further submits that in view of the fact that the impugned decree is not such a decree as in a partition suit and the award, which was not a registered one, was not evidently executable per se and consequently the action of the learned Advocate Commissioner in dispossessing the petitioners from the suit property in exercise of the purported power given to him by the Execution Court is illegal and consequently the petitioners have no other efficacious remedy available to them for redress of their grievance and, as such, they are entitled to get relief by way of restoration of possession by resorting to the provision of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Advocate further submits that in view of the fact that the action of the learned Advocate Commissioner dispossessing the petitioners from their suit property causing them irreparable loss and injury and the writ of delivery of possession was evidently an error of law committed by the learned Execution Court in purported execution of an inexecutable decree, the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in refusing relief to the petitioners under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the same has occasioned failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Subordinate Judge also erred in law in not properly appreciating the scope of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in asking the petitioners to initiate independent proceedings for redress of their grievance on an erroneous view of law and the same has occasioned a failure of justice. 

 8. Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties, on the other hand, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge was perfectly justified in passing the impugned order on assigning cogent and sound reasons and consequently the impugned order does not suffer from any illegality occasioning failure of justice so as to justify interference by this Court exercising revisional jurisdiction under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Fazlul Karim further submits that in view of the provision of Order 21 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure the executing Court has ample power to appoint Commissioner for executing a decree and if the petitioners really feel aggrieved by the action of the learned Advocate Commissioner, they are required to place the matter before the learned. Court by challenging the decree itself but instead of doing so, they invoked the application of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which is not maintainable in law. Mr. Fazlul Karim submits that on detailed discussion and proper appreciation of the materials on record, the learned Subordinate Judge rightly passed the impugned order as in the facts of the case there is no scope for giving any relief to the petitioners under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and consequently the petitioners are not entitled to get any relief in the case. 

 11. The submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite parties that the petitioners had other remedy available to them for redressing their grievance and as such they are not entitled to get any relief under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not amenable to reason, justice and good conscience. 

 16. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs and the impugned order dated 19-10-97 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat Court No. 4, Dhaka in Title Execution Case No. 20 of 1997 rejecting the petitioners' application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of possession in the suit land is set aside. Accordingly, the petitioners' application for restoration under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is allowed. In view of the fact that the petitioners were dispossessed from the suit property by the learned Advocate Commissioner in pursuance of the order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in Title Execution Case No. 20 of 1997, I find no difficulty in restoration of possession to the petitioners. The learned Subordinate Judge is accordingly directed to restore to the petitioners possession of the suit property from where they were dispossessed by the learned Advocate Commissioner on 18-6-97 in execution of the writ issued to him by the learned Executing Court.

parties:
Mokarram Hossain and others ------ Petitioners
Vs.
ADC (Rev) Pabna for Vested and Non-Resident Property (Land and Building) Pabna & others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This revision at the instance of the plaintiff of Title suit 232 of 1984, for declaration of title and it is against the judgment and decree dated 30-10-1995 passed in Title Appeal No.1l9 of 1986 by the Additional District Judge, Pabna dismissing the appeal which was taken by the plaintiff. Trial Court also dismissed the suit by his judgment dated 8-3-1986. 

 2. Plaintiffs suit, in short, is that the suit land belonged to Suphir Kumar Lahiri. Abdul Gafur took settlement of the suit land from said Suphir Kumar Lahiri on 10th Asar 1353 BS. Abdur Gafur filed Other Class suit No. 178 of 1969 for declaration of his title and got an ex parte decree. Plaintiff has purchased the suit land from said Abdul Gafur in the year 1980 and got possession in the suit land and he is still holding ownership. The suit land, according to the plaintiff, was wrongly recorded in the name of Suphir Kumar Lahiri in SA Khatian and, as such, it was listed illegally as vested and non-resident property in case No. 159 of 1966-67. So the suit has been filed for declaration of title. Defendant Government contested by filing written statement.Defendant's case is that Suphir Kumar Lahiri, the original owner of the suit land, left this country in the year 1965 and, as such, the suit property was made at first enemy property vide enemy property case in 1965-68 and thereafter vested and non-resident property in the aforesaid case made on 20-2-82. Abdul Gafur got a fraudulent ex parte decree in his said Other Class suit No.178 of 1969 collusively and subsequently the plaintiff obtained the deed of purchase of the suit land fraudulently and collusively which does not impart any title to the plaintiff. It is on record that the suit property was made enemy property by order dated 3-12-65 in EP case No. 195. Subsequently it, by operation of law, became vested and non-resident property. Ext. (A) shows that Abdul Gafur vendor of the plaintiff had knowledge of the same. The plaintiff himself also knew the same. Subsequent transfer by Abdul Gafur to the plaintiff is therefore fraudulent one and without lawful authority. The plaintiff and other persons unsuccessfully tried to get release of the property alleging that they took pattan from Suphir Kumar Lahiri. 

 3. Mr. Md Nawab Ali, tried to plead adverse possession on behalf of the plaintiff. Since the defendant opposite party is Government so adverse possession against the Government unless 60 years over, cannot be claimed which is not there in the instant case, plaintiffs possession is however admitted by the defendant. But possession of the plaintiff in the aforesaid circumstance has not created any title by adverse possession. Both the Courts below legally and rightly found on appreciation of the evidence on record that the plaintiff failed to prove his title. Original plaintiff Abul Hossain has died. His minor sons and daughters and wife are residents in the homestead situated on the suit land which is 0.0900 Ajutansha. It is stated by Mr. Noab Ali that the plaintiffs have no other land to live upon. 

 "No eviction from Homestead. Any land used as a homestead by its owner in the rural area shall be excepted from all legal processes including seizure, distress, attachment or sale by any officer; Court or any other authority and the owner of such land shall not be divested or dispossessed of the land or evicted therefrom by any means. Although the plaintiffs have no title because they possess the suit land on the basis of some documents, which are not valid, as correctly found by the Courts below. But they cannot be evicted from their homestead situated on the suit land in view of the provision of section 6 of Act 10 of 1984 as referred above. And if the property in the suit is given lease by the Government the plaintiffs shall be given first preference".

parties:
Sonali Bank  ----- Appellant
Vs.
Beg and Beg Jute Mills Ltd and others ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal J: The question raised in this appeal by leave by the plaintiff-appellant Sonali Bank is, whether in the instant mortgage suit for sale the plaintiff is also entitled as of law to a decree for interest both pendente lite and till realisation of the decretal amount. 

 2. The Appellant-Bank instituted Title Suit No. 31 of 1983 (later re-numbered as Title Suit No. 131 of 1984) originally in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, later transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 2, Dhaka which was a suit for recovery of money by sale of mortgaged property for a preliminary decree for Taka 14,00,000.00 with interest at 20% till realisation with a direction that the Schedule property be sold on failure to pay the decretal amount and to make the preliminary decree final on failure to pay as aforesaid and also praying for a personal decree against the defendants for the said amount. The Commercial Court decreed that suit for an amount of Taka 8,85,485.39 payable in quarterly instalments of Taka 50,000.00 but allowed no interest as prayed for, by judgment and decree dated 24-12-86. The appellant-Bank took an appeal to the High Court Division, FA No. 91 of 1987, against the said decree on the ground that interest on the decretal amount pendente lite and till realisation was wrongly refused by the trial Court. By the impugned judgment dated 1-4-90 a Division Bench of the High Court Division dismissed the said appeal holding that the Commercial Court had exercised its discretion in refusing interest to the plaintiff on the decretal amount on valid ground. 

 11. Dr Rafiqur Rahman, learned Counsel for the respondents, has made a feeble attempt to show that the suit was in fact for a personal decree against the Managing Director and other Directors and that it does not fulfill the characteristics of a mortgage suit. Having gone through the plaint and decree passed in the suit under Order 34 rule 4(1) CPC we have no manner of doubt whatsoever that this is a mortgage suit for sale and a preliminary decree has to be drawn up in terms of rule 4(1), read with rule 2(1) in the manner mentioned in clauses (a), (b) and (c)(i) thereof. The plaintiff-Bank obtained a mortgage by deposit of title deeds. A mortgage by deposit of title deeds being placed on the same footing as a simple mortgage (section 96 of the Transfer of Property Act) the only remedy is a suit for sale which the plaintiff-bank availed of in the instant case. 

 23. We therefore hold that the High Court Division acted illegally in not holding that the plaintiff-appellant was entitled to interest pendente lite, ie, from the date of the institution of the suit upto the date of the passing of the decree. 

 25. The original agreement between the parties is that the defendants will pay interest at 2¼% above Bank rate, the minimum being 10½%. Subsequently on an extension of the cash credit facilities the rate of interest was increased to 13½%. In the plaint the plaintiff has asked for interest at the rate of 20% pendente lite.

parties:
Rabiul Alam and another ------ Petitioner 
vs.
Sree Bidhan Kumar Deb, Advocate ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
4. The plaintiffs' case in short is that the suit premises originally belonged to one Binodi Lal Biswas a practising Mukhtiar at Dinajpur and the plaintiffs acquired the same from the said Binodi Lal Biswaw in exchange of their Indian property Binodi Lal Biswas executed a power of attorney in favour of the plaintiffs in respect of the suit premises and some other properties. The aforesaid document was registered as deed No. 8058 on 12-5-1961 at the Sub-Registry Office of Dinajpur. The plaintiffs first let out the suit premises to Bibhuti Bhusan Deb father of the defendant and after Bibhutis death in 1971 let out the premises to the defendant at a monthly rent of Taka 30.00 from March, 1972 and  subsequently the rent was enhanced to Taka 60.00 per month. The defendant was a monthly tenant under the plaintiffs in respect of the suit premises. He regularly paid rent to the plaintiffs upto March, 1979 and thereafter, he defaulted. The defendant was a habitual defaulter. The plaintiffs were in bonafide requirement of the suit premises for their own use as plaintiff No. 1 Rabiul Alam subsequently became an Advocate. The plaintiffs issued notice under section 106 and 111 of the Transfer of Property Act by registered post to the defendant through their lawyer determining the relationship of landlord and tenant and demanding vacant possession of the suit premises on the expiry of the Month of September, 1982. The defendant received the notice in time but did not vacate the premises hence the suit. 

 5. The defendant opposite party contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations and assertions made in the plaint stating inter alia that the plaintiffs had no cause of action: that the suit was not maintainable; that the SCC Judge had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit; that there was no relationship of landlord and tenant between them; that the suit was bad for defect of parties;: that the plaintiffs had no right, title and interest in the suit premises; that Benodi Lal Biswas the original owner of the suit property abandoned the same as some ghostly occurrence took place in the said house and lived in a nearby house; that having found the house vacant the defendant's father Bibhuti Bhusan entered into the said house in 1947 just after the partition and lived therein with his family till his death in 1971; that the defendant was neither a tenant nor a licencee under anybody; that after the death of his father the defendant and the members of his family continued to live in the suit premises, that Binodi Lal left Dinajpur for India that in collusion with some influential persons the plaintiffs forged a power of attorney purported to have been executed by Binodi Lal Biswas in order to grab the valuable property, that after the promulgation of Martial Law in 1975 Kotwali Police having been influenced by the plaintiffs threatened the defendant with dispossession and eviction if they failed to recognise the plaintiffs as their landlord; that in order to avoid forcible eviction the defendant put his signature on a rent receipt and recognised the plaintiffs as his landlords and once he deposited Taka 40.00 only with the House Rent Controller in favour of the plaintiffs but subsequently withdrew the said case; that the ADC (Rev) Dinajpur illegally executed a deed of exchange for registration in favour of the plaintiffs; that the  plaintiffs have no right title interest and possession in the suit premises and hence the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 6. The learned SCC Judge framed as many as 6 issues namely 1) was the suit maintainable in its present form 2) was the defendant a tenant under the plaintiffs 3) was the defendant a habitual defaulter 4) were the plaintiffs in bonafide requirement of the suit premises 5) had the plaintiffs incidental title in the suit premises and 6) what other relief or reliefs were the plaintiffs entitled to? The plaintiffs examined 4 PWs in support of their case while the defendant examined 8 DWs and having considered the evidence on record the learned SCC Judge by judgment and order dated 30-6-87 returned the plaint for filing in the proper court holding inter alia that he defendant did not attorne the plaintiffs as his landlords, that there was no relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties that the suit was bad for defect of parties, and that the suit was not maintainable as a complicated question of title was involved in the suit and thus decided almost all the vital issues against the plaintiffs 

 9. Mr Wahab further submits that having got the deed of exchange validated the plaintiffs mutated their names and paid rent (Ext. 3) and in that view of the matter the defendant who is a tenant under the plaintiffs is estopped from challenging the title of the plaintiffs and in support of this contention Mr Wahab cited the case of Haji Kasimuddin Mondal being dead his heirs Afroza Bewa and others vs. Md Jalaluddin Pramanik reported in 48 DLR (AD) 205. In the reported case it was held: 

 "In the instant case the suit is in essence and substantially a suit by the landlord for ejectment of his tenant. In such a case the question of title to the disputed premises is not relevant at all. Once a relationship of landlord and tenant is pleaded by the plaintiff the landlord cannot be thrown out of the Court of Small Causes on the plea of tenant's title on which the landlord's claim does not depend." 

 10. In the instant case the tenant does not claim title for himself rather he sets up a case that Binodi Lal never executed any deed of exchange in favour of the plaintiffs. In the reported case their Lordships further held that in the face of overwhelming evidence that there was relationship of landlord and tenant between the plaintiffs and the defendant the defendant could not raise any plea of the title to the disputed premises. It has been consistently held by the superior courts including this court that a tenant cannot set up title to a property of which he is a monthly tenant without surrendering possession to his landlord in view of section 116 of the Evidence Act. If the landlord can prove, as in the instant case, that the defendant was inducted by him on the disputed premises or that the defendant has attorned to him and has continued in possession on payment of rent after recognising him as the landlord he cannot turn round and deny the title of the said landlord. Reference may be made in this connection to the case of Abdus Sauar vs. Mohiuddin 38 DLR (AD) 97. His Lordship Mr Shahabuddin Ahmed J as his Lordship then was expounded the principle of law embodied in section 116 of the Evidence Act which runs thus; 

 Section 116 " The estoppel as described in this section is known as tenant's estoppel or estoppel by contract. This estoppel is founded upon a contract between the tenant and the landlord. It provides that when a person enters into possession of immovable property as a tenant of another person then neither he nor anybody claiming through him shall be permitted during the continuance of the tenancy to deny the landlord's title however defective that title might be. This necessarily implies that in case the tenant sets up a claim of title in himself he shall firstly surrender possession to the person from whom he had taken it." 

 11. Mr Muhammad Jamiruddin Sircar, learned Counsel appearing for the opposite party submits that in view of the finding of the trial Court that the case involved a question of title the same should not be tried by the SCC, Court rather by a competent civil court. But on a reference to the evidence and the documents mentioned above I am unable to accept this contention of the learned Counsel for the opposite party inasmuch as the suit being between an alleged landlord and an alleged tenant for enforcement of certain rights of the landlord the simple question which is to be tried in such a suit is whether there is existence of any relationship of a landlord and a tenant as has been established by PWs 3.4 and 5 inasmuch as by the rent receipt Ext. 5 series and the House Rent Countrol case filed by the defendant being Misc. Case No. 97 of 1997 (Rent Control) it was proved that the defendant was a tenant under the plaintiffs. In such a case the question of title to the premises in question is not relevant at all. The position of law is based upon the rule of evidence regarding the doctrine of estoppel as embodied in section 116 of the Evidence Act which has been elaborately discussed in 48 DLR(AD) 205. 

 14. Now coming to the judgment of the trial Court I find that almost all the issues were decided against the plaintiffs and coming to the issue as to whether the suit is maintainable the trial Court found that since there is a question of title involved it should he decided by competent civil court and accordingly returned the plaint for filing the same in the proper court. Section 23 of the Small Cause Courts Act provides as follows: 

 "23. Return of plaints in suits involving questions of title- 

 (1) Notwithstanding anything in the foregoing portion of this Act when the right of a plaintiff and the relief claimed by him in a Court of Small Causes depend upon the proof or the learned court is contrary to the provision of disproof of a title to immovable property or other title which such a Court cannot finally determine the Court may at any stage of the proceedings return the plaint to be presented to a Court having jurisdiction to determine the title." 

 15. From a reading of section 23 of the Small Cause Courts Act it is clear that the word May in section 23 is not mandatory. When in a suit heard by a Small Cause Court any complicated question as to title to immovable property is involved it would be wiser course to act under section 23 as decided in the case of Lala Singh vs. Mohipal Singh 1889 AWN 149. But in the instant case I do not find any question of title involved let alone a complicated question of title because the tenant himself does not set up a title for himself, he merely alleges that the original owner Benodi Lal did not exchange the property with the plaintiffs. The trial Court held that mere payment of rent is no recognition by the tenant of his landlord but as has already been referred to the signature appearing in Ext. 4 ie chircuit   is exactly the same as in Ext. 5 (21), 5(29) and 5(39). 

 17. Paragraph 14 of the written statement. Ext 4 the chircuit (চিরকুট) the rent receipt Ext. 5(21), 5 ,22) and 5(29), Misc. Case No. 97 of 1979 (Rent Control) Ext. 10(a) read together have made in a clear case of admission by the defendant that the plaintiffs are his landlord and, as such, he is estopped  from denying the plaintiffs title to the premises and in support of this contention Mr MA Wahab Miah learned Counsel for the petitioners cited the case of Hajee Abdus Sattar VS. Mahiuddin and ors reported in 1986 BLD(AD) 224. 

 18. Having considered the facts circumstances, the evidence on record and the exhibits referred to above, I am of the opinion that the plaintiffs were able to prove the relationship of landlord and tenant between themselves and the defendant Bidhan Kumar and there being no complicated question of title involved the trial Court was wrong in returning the plaint for filing the same in a proper court and hence the impugned order calls for interference by this court.

Abdul Mannan Miah (Md) ----- Petitioner

full_judgment:

parties:
Kashem Khan (Md) & others ----- Petitioners.
Vs.
Sudarshan Singh ----- Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
Md. Joynul Abedin J: This Rule at the instance of the defendants-petitioners calls in question the judgment and decree dated 19-5-96 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayanganj in Title Appeal No. 61 of 1994 affirming the judgment and decree dated 18-5-94 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Narayanganj in Title Suit No. 159 of 1990 decreeing the suit declaring title of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 to the suit land on the basis of adverse possession. 

 2. Plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 filed the aforesaid suit praying for declaration of his title to the suit land on the basis of adverse possession alleging, inter alia, that one Satish Chandra Saha was the owner of .36 decimals of land appertaining to CS Khatian No. 318 and CS plot No. 426 of MouzaKhanpur 'Ma' Khanda under PS and District-Narayanganj. Similarly said Satish Chandra Saha was also the owner of .28 decimals of land of CS plot No. 425 of the same Khatian and mouza. Since most of the aforesaid land was diches and unused land said Satish Chandra Saha never enjoyed the same by taking physical possession thereof. The father of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 Kailash Chandra Singh took over possession of the suit land measuring .05 decimal to the north-east portion of CS plot No. 426 and developed the same and constructed two tin-shed huts by investing his own money and used to reside in one tin-shed with his family and the other hut was used by him as his grocery-Lakri shop since the middle of 1940. After about 2 months thereof the said Satish Chandra Saha found the father of plaintiff-opposite party No.1 in the suit land and asked him to vacate the same or he would take necessary action for evicting him by force therefrom. Inspite of such threat, the father of plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 continued in possession of the suit land within the knowledge of the said Satish Chandra Saha. Subsequently the father of the plaintiff-opposite party repaired his residential hut and extended his shop by investing more money and rented it out to various persons and received rent from them. In this way the father of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 enjoyed the possession of the suit land adversely against the said Salish Chandra Saha for more than 12 years since he took ever possession of the same in the middle of 1940 till he died in 1967 leaving behind plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 as his only heir. Thereafter the plaintif-opposite party No. 1 continued in possession of the suit land. Defendant No. 2 being the managing director of defendant No. 1, which is a commercial concern, held out a threat in February, 1988 to dispossess the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 disclosing that defendant No. 1 purchased the entire .64 decimals of land appertaining to plot Nos. 426 and 425 of the said mouza including the suit land by a sale deed in 1951 from to said Satish Chandra Saha. In this pack ground of the matter, plaintiff-oppositee party No. 1 was compelled to file the present suit for declaration of his title to the suit land on the basis of adverse possession. 

 3. Defendant Nos. 3 to 10 and 11 contested the suit by filing separate written statement. The defendant No. 3 to 10 contended in their written statement that their predecessors-in-interest constructed various structures on the aforesaid 2 suit plots for the purpose of their residence and for carrying on business. During their possession of the suit plots in the above manner defendant Nos. 1 and 2 demanded rent from their predecessors claiming that they became owners of the suit plots by virtue of purchase of the same from Satish Chandra Saha. In order to avoid litigations the predecessors of defendant Nos. 3 to 10 agreed to buy lands of the suit plots and in the process defendant Nos. 1 and 2 received Taka. 5000.00 on 10-2-69 and Taka. 1,5000.00 on 19-3-69 by way of advance. But since defendant Nos. 1 and 2 failed to execute and register necessary sale deed their predecessors filed Title Suit No: 33 of 1970 for specific performance contract against defendant Nos. 1 and 2 which is still pending. Defendant No. 11 being the Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Narayanganj contended in its written statement that the suit plots belonged to one Mariam Sattar, a non-Bengali and she left this country in 1971 during the liberation war and the suit plots became abandoned property and thus vested in the Government by operation of PO 16 of 1972 and as such the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 had no right, title and interest in the suit land and the suit was liable to be dismissed. 

 4. Plaintiff-opposite party No.1 examined 4 PWs in support of his case including himself as PW 1. On the other hand defendant Nos. 3 to 10 examined 3 PWs and one DW was examined as DW 4 on 'behalf of defendant No. 11. The trial Court after due scrutiny and assessment of the evidence on record believed the case of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 and decreed the suit. Defendant Nos. 3 to 10 thereafter preferred Title Appeal No. 61 of 1994 against the said judgment and decree dated 18-5-94 of the trial Court to the District Judge, Narayanganj. The Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Narayanganj by the impugned judgment and decree affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court on due assessment and scrutiny of the evidence and matterials on record. 

 5. Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioners contends that since schedule to the plaint does not contain necessary description to identify the suit land, the decree given on the basis of such description is not sustainable in law. In support of his contention the learned Advocate-refers to the decision in the case of Noor Mohammad Khan vs. The Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others reported in 42 DLR 434. The learned Advocate next contends that the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside for non-consideration of material evidence namely Exts. Ka to Ja except Ext. Cha in this case. The learned Advocate MrAlam further contends that the impugned judgment and decree are also liable to be set aside for omitting Satish Chandra Saha, being the original owner of the suit plot, to be impleaded as a defendant to this suit and also for not giving a finding on fact as to the adverse possession of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 on proper scrutiny of the evidence on record. 

 6. Mr Kh Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 submits that the contentions raised by the learned Advocate of the defendant-petitioner have no merit. Mr Ahmed further submits that the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 has given sufficient descriptions of the suit land both in the plaint and in his evidence to identify the suit land. The learned Advocate also submits that both the courts below found on due consideration of the evidence on record adduced by both the parties that the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 acquired title and interest in the suit land by advrese possession against the original owner of the suit land. 

 8. It appears from the impugned judgment of the Courts below, particularly the trial Court that the Courts below, considered the material evidence adduced by both the parties and came to the finding that the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 had been in uninterrupted possession of the suit land through his father and himself for more than 2 years since the middle of 1940 and thus acquired title in the suit land by adverce possession thereof against the original owner. Therefore, the contention of the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners that the decree given in the suit suffers from non-consideration of material evidence and also for want of a finding by the courts below that the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 acquired title in the suit land by adverse possession has no substance. 

 9. With regard to the contention of the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioners that the decree in the instant suit is liable to be dismissed for the failure of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 to implead the original owner Satish Chandra Saha is also not acceptable to us inasmuch as such omission did not prejudice the defendant-petitioners, more so when it was disclosed in the plaint that whereabouts of Satish Chandra Saha was not known. 

 12. When a judge hears and secs witnesses and makes a conclusion or inference with regard to what is the weight on balance of their evidence, that judgment is entitled to great respect irrespective of whether the judge makes any observation with regard to credibility or not. 

 13. On careful consideration of the contentions raised on behalf of the parties we do not find that the courts below have committed any error of law resulting in an error in the impugned judgment and decree occasioning failure of justice in this case. In the result, the Rule is discharged and the impugned judgment and decree dated 19-5-1996 passed in Title Appeal No. 61 of 1994 affirming the judgment and decree dated 18-5-1994 passed in Title Suit No. 159 of 1990 is hereby confirmed without any order as to costs.

Mohammad Gholam Rabbani, J: This Rule has been obtained by petitioner Md. Nur Hossain for analogous hearing of the five suits pending in three different civil courts at Dhaka in respect of same property situated within P.S. Subujbag of the City of Dhaka. Opposite party No. 10 Mcd. Delowar Hossain in this Rule has instituted Title Suit No. 137 of 1993 in the 3rd court of subordinate judge for declaration of his title to the suit property. Opposite party No. 9 Jahura Begum in this rule has instituted Title Suit No. 131 of 1993 in the 4th court of Assistant judge for declaration of her title to the suit property petitioner in this rule has instituted two suits one being Title Suit No. 71 of 1993 in the 3rd Additional Court of Assistant judge, for permanent injunction in respect of the suit property, and the other being title suit No. 309 of 1989 in the 4th court of Assistant judge for declaration of title to the suit property. Opposite party Zahura .Begum obtained an ex-parte decree in title suit No. 44 of 1988 from the 4th court of Assistant Judge and put the decree in execution in Execution Case No. 1 of 1993. However, the ex-parte decree was set aside and title suit No. 44 of 1988 was restored to its original file and number and the suit is now pending. In this rule petitioner prays that all the suits be tried analogously by one court. 

 3. Since the parties are litigating claiming title to the same property by filing several suits, justice demands that all the stilts should be tried analogously by one court and as such objection of the learned advocate for the opposite party No. 9 is not acceptable. 

 5. It is ordered that all the suits, namely Title Suit No. 137 or 1993 pending in the 3rd court of Subordinate judge Dhaka, title Suit No. 71 of 1993 Pending in the 3rd Additional court of Assistant judge Dhaka title suit No. 131 of 1993 pending in the 4th court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka Title Suit No. 37 of 1992 pending in the 4th court of Assistant Judge. Dhaka and title Suit No. 44 of 1988 pending in the 4th court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka and title Suit No. 44 of 1988 pending in the 4th court of Assistant judge, Dhaka shall be tried analogously by the 3rd court of Subordinate judge. full_judgment:
Md. Abdur Rouf J: Late Khalilur Rahman Sarder, predecessor-in-interest of respondent Nos.1-4 instituted Title Suit No.144 of 1986, in the Court of Assistant Judge, Shariatpur, for declaration of title to 90 decimals of land on the averments, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to defendant No.1, the present appellant, Narayan Chandra Dey and that the plaintiff purchased the same in public auction on 30-12-62 sold in a Certificate Case, under the Public Demands Recovery Act, for arrears of rent. The sale was confirmed and the sale Certificate was issued on 27-12-1963. The plaintiff was put into possession on 19-8-1963 and since then he has been possessing the suit land. On 23-11-1986 he sold 45 decimals of land out of the suit land to defendant No. 3 who after constructing houses thereon has also been residing there. In the middle of Agrahayan 1393 BS defendant No. 1 gave out threat to dispossess him from the suit land. 

 5. The heirs of the original plaintiff (respondent Nos.1-4) preferred appeal, Title Appeal No. 35 of 1992, and the learned Subordinate Judge, Shariatpur by his judgment and decree dated 3-11-93 allowed the appeal, set aside the decree of the trial Court and decreed the suit holding, inter alia, that defendant No.1 (appellant) could not discharge his onus to prove that the documents relating to the auction purchase are forged and collusive. The appellant then moved the High Court Division in revision against the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court, Civil Revision No. 1191 of 1994, which was summarily rejected by a Single Bench of the High Court Division on 16-1-94. Leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division erred in law in rejecting the revisional application summarily when the judgment of the lower appellate Court, a judgment of reversal, does not patently show that it reversed in the trial Court's finding on possession of the appellant in the disputed land and also does not show that it adverted to the trial Court's reasoning for disbelieving Ext. 1, 1(Ka), 3 and 3(Ka) as to the alleged certificate sale of the suit land. 

 The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division as well as the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court passed by the Subordinate Judge, Shariatpur in Title Appeal No. 35 of 1992 on 3-11-93 are set aside and the appeal is sent back to the lower appellate Court for rehearing in accordance with law.

caseno:
Civil Revision No. 235 of 1985 (Rangpur) 
Civil Revision No.3981 of 1991 (Dhaka)
parties:
Jamila Khatun ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Md Lutfor Rahman @ Nefasiur and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This is an application for addition of party. Applicants were not made parties before the trial Court although the alleged land was purchased by them from opposite party No. 1 by different Kabalas during pendency of the suit before the trial Court. The record shows that the original suit was for declaration of three kabalas are void and illegal. On those kabalas defendant Nos. 1 and 2 purchased the suit land. So the suit is not for declaration of title to those kabalas land. 

 2. Mr. Akram Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate, submitted on behalf of the petitioner-opposite party that there is no bar to add the petitioners as party for they have interest in the subject matter of the suit indirectly and that they did not pray for adding as party before the court below as their vendors contested the suit thereon and being failed in the court below he preferred a Revisional application before this court. He further submitted that since the petitioners are being prejudiced as their predecessor has filed a compromise petition with the opposite party in the Revisional application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In support of his contention he referred to a case reported in 21 DLR 190 and also a case reported in 43 DLR 7. In both the cases Single Bench of our High Court took the view that the doctrine of lis pendens does not make alienations made during pendency of a suit void but only that such alienation will not affect the rights of other parties to the suit. It has already been stated above that the original suit was not for a declaration of title. It is for declarations of three deeds are illegal and void. The petitioner purchased the land of those disputed Kabalas during pendency of the suit before the trial Court. So, the petitioners claim is hit by the doctrine of lis pendens. In this respect the learned Advocate for the opposite party of this petition submitted that the petitioner is neither a necessary party nor their presence are necessary in this suit as the subject matter of the suit is not the purchased land and that they can not be added as party to this application in any way. In support of his contention he referred to a case reported in 32 DLR 63 wherein their Lordships took the view that "A transfer of the land in suit being the subject-matter of the pending suit is hit by the doctrine of lis pendens and, as such, such a transfer is not valid in law. And consequently such a transferee cannot apply under Order 1, rule 10(2) CPC to be impleaded as a party to the suit." In the instant petition the petitioners purchased the disputed land during pendency of the suit from the persons against whose sale deeds the suit was filed. Since the petitioners are subsequent purchasers they are neither a necessary party to the suit nor their presence is necessary to decide this type of suit. On the above discussion I find no substance in this application and, as such, the application for adding as party is rejected.
